Part Two: Clarifying the Meaning of Severing and Subduing. This section has two parts: first, clarifying severing and subduing; second, discussing miscellaneous questions and answers.

First, the clarification of abandonment and suppression has three parts: first, the clarification of abandonment and suppression; second, the discussion of cultivation; and third, the differentiation of gain and loss.

Regarding the first, the clarification of the meaning of abandonment and suppression, it is explained briefly as in the section on the meaning of awakening from a dream. Here, it is clarified by way of the stages (*bhūmi*).

The masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Shí dì yì chéng shí lùn shī) trace their lineage back to the *Vyavahāra-vibhāga* school (Zhuāngyán jiā). During the two dynasties of Northern Zhou and Northern Qi, the meaning of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* was widely elucidated.
Although this doctrine had been flourishing for some time, it was later, during the era of the two Tripiṭaka masters Bodhiruci and Ratnamati, that the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* was translated;
the merit of this achievement thus belongs to these two masters. Now, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* provides an exposition of the stages (*bhūmi*) regarding what is abandoned and what is suppressed.
The meanings differ. First, the *Zhuāngyán jiā* (Ornament School) states that the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be subdued are briefly of four kinds:

first, afflictions regarding the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*); second, those regarding cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); third, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); and fourth, ignorance (*ajñāna*). These four types of afflictions are divided into ten categories;

the afflictions of the vision of the truths are further divided into three—namely, superior, middling, and inferior grades—speaking in terms of the majority, and taking the superior grade as the primary example.
One is born in hell through the superior grade; the middling grade invites rebirth as an animal; and the inferior grade leads to falling among the spirits (preta). This is as stated in the treatise.
Taking deliberation (*vitarka*) as the three grades, these are bound to the three realms: the station of craving for the desire realm (*kāmarāga-vihāra-bhūmi*) is the superior grade;

the station of craving for the form realm (*rūparāga-vihāra-bhūmi*) is the middling grade; and the station of craving for existence (*bhavarāga-vihāra-bhūmi*) is the inferior grade. These stations of deliberation bound to the three realms must necessarily—

"Different" means not the same. Seeing the Truth (*satyadarśana*) eradicates the three miserable realms; this is spoken of from the perspective of the majority. Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are the remnants of the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
therefore, they need not be distinguished separately and are combined into one category. The Dwelling Ground of Ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā-bhūmi*) possesses the strongest power;

it can obstruct profound practice and takes the longest time to sever. Furthermore, in terms of phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is divided into three distinctions, namely: form (*rūpa*)... [text fragment ends].

Ignorance regarding the objective field (*viṣaya*) is considered the superior grade; ignorance regarding the mind (*citta*) is considered the middling grade; and ignorance regarding the arising of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) is considered the inferior grade.
While these three types of ignorance truly possess degrees of coarseness and subtlety, for the sake of following the majority of cases, they are explained as previously stated.
Within these four categories, they are further divided into ten grades and subdued through ten stages. The first stage is prior to the [ten] grounds (*bhūmi*).
The first ten moments of mind subdue the superior grade of the truths of vision (*satyadarśana*). The second, middle ten moments of mind subdue the middle grade of the truths of vision.

The third, final ten moments of mind subdue the inferior grade of the truths of vision. The fourth, the initial stage (*bhūmi*), subdues the conceptualization (*vitarka*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

The fifth, the second stage, subdues the conceptualization of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The sixth, the third stage, subdues the conceptualization of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The seventh, the fourth...
The stages (*bhūmi*) can suppress the remaining habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). On the eighth and fifth stages, one suppresses the ignorance regarding material objects (*rūpa-viṣaya-ajñāna*);

on the ninth and sixth stages, one suppresses the ignorance regarding the difficulty of the mind; and on the seventh stage, one suppresses the ignorance regarding the arising of formations (*saṃskāra-samudaya-ajñāna*).

As for why it is necessarily discussed that the afflictions of the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) are exhausted prior to the stages: the transition from an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) to a noble one (*ārya*) is truly difficult. This is because the vision of the truths is contrary to the Noble Path.

If these afflictions have been subdued, one may enter the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*); if they have not yet reached that limit, it is impossible to attain the Way. The path of abandonment (*prahāṇamārga*) likewise consists of ten stages:

the first stage abandons the superior grade of the truths to be seen (*satyadarśana*); the second stage abandons the middle grade of the truths to be seen; the third stage abandons the inferior grade of the truths to be seen;

the fourth stage abandons the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the desire realm; the fifth stage abandons the cultivation of the form realm; the sixth [stage abandons the cultivation of the formless realm]...

The first stage (bhūmi) eliminates the conceptualization of the formless; the seventh stage eliminates habitual tendencies (vāsanā); the eighth stage eliminates ignorance regarding material objects (rūpa-viṣaya); the ninth stage eliminates ignorance regarding the difficulty of the mind;

and the tenth stage eliminates ignorance regarding the arising of the aggregates (saṃskāra). Quoting the Great Master Liang’s commentary on the *Shengshengzhong* (The Arising Within Arising), it says:

"In the third dwelling, the views of the truths (satyadarśana-heya) are exhausted; in the fourth dwelling, the conceptualizations of the desire realm (kāmadhātu-bhāvanā-heya) are exhausted. Kaishan and others say that this occurs in the sixth stage.
At the end of this, one’s merit will surely equal that of an Arhat; thus, the fetters of the formless realm are exhausted, which is the intended meaning of the *Ratnavyuha-sūtra* (瓔珞經).

Furthermore, it should be understood that at the fifth stage (*bhūmi*), the contemplative afflictions (*vitarka*) of the form realm are exhausted. The School of Adornment (*Zhuāngyán jiā*) states: "The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (十住論) says that the delusions of view (*darśana-heya*) are exhausted in the first stage.
This meaning correctly refers to the ability to sever the delusions of the truths (*satya-darśana*), not that they are entirely exhausted. It is like [the case of] the Srotāpanna.

When one attains the vision of the truths (satyadarśana), the outflows are exhausted and one will certainly reach nirvāṇa. This is likened to being born into the family of the Buddha upon reaching the first stage (bhūmi);
thus, one gives rise to joy through contemplation. This is merely a partial analogy; it does not mean that the vision of the truths is entirely completed at the first stage.

As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, since one has already severed the afflictions of the three realms (tridhātu) through cultivation (bhāvanā) at the first stage, could it be said that the afflictions of cultivation are entirely exhausted at the first stage? Therefore, we know [that this is not the case].

This means that while the bonds of the truths have been severed, they are not yet exhausted. Furthermore, it is said that because there is a distinction between specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and ignorance (*ajñāna*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) must necessarily be coarse, whereas ignorance must necessarily be subtle. That which is coarse is eliminated first; that which is subtle is severed later.

Since ignorance is correctly severed from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one knows that habitual tendencies are exhausted within the seventh stage. Thus, it is said: "From the first stage to the seventh..."

Regarding "the stages can subdue and sever": on the first stage (*bhūmi*), one severs the views regarding the truth (*satyadarśana*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and simultaneously subdues the conceptualizations (*vitarka*) of the desire realm.

On the second stage, one correctly severs the views regarding the truth of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and simultaneously subdues the conceptualizations of the form realm. On the third stage, one correctly severs the views regarding the truth of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and simultaneously subdues the conceptualizations of the formless realm.
On the fourth stage, one correctly severs the ground of abiding in craving for desire (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*). This is the profound [meaning].

One subdues the ignorance and the myriad afflictions beyond the three realms; in the fifth stage, one correctly severs the ground of attachment to form and fully subdues the ignorance regarding the objects of form.
In the sixth stage, one correctly severs the ground of attachment to existence and immediately fully subdues the ignorance regarding the difficulty of the mind.

On the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one eradicates the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). This refers to the thorough suppression of the collective arising of form and mind.
From the first stage through the seventh, one both eradicates and suppresses; from the eighth stage upward, one only eradicates and does not suppress. The remaining phrases may be sought elsewhere.

Second, the *Shaozhuangyan Longguang Zhuan* (The Tradition of Longguang’s Concise Adornment) explains the doctrine of Kaishan: some say that the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are completely eradicated at the third stage, while others say [it occurs] at the first...

Regarding the severance of the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa*), although it is exhausted across all stages, it is primarily associated with the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Therefore, Kaishan asked [the masters] Baoneng and others:

according to the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Yingluo jing), "Because a Bodhisattva of the first stage severs the delusions of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*)," and the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* likewise states, "In the first stage, the delusions of the truths are exhausted.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva of the second stage severs the afflictions among humans, while a Bodhisattva of the third stage severs...
Regarding the afflictions of the heavens: Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage (*bhūmi*) sever the afflictions from the third dhyāna downward;

Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage sever the afflictions from the three emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) downward; Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage sever the afflictions that are neither characterized by signs nor signless.

Therefore, among the delusions of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*), the delusions of the latter four abodes are also included therein. This is the traditional interpretation. That [text] refers to them as the "four abodes."

The delusions (*moha*) and the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vitarka-kleśa*) do not have distinct essential natures; they are merely designated differently by the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.

According to the doctrinal tenets of Dharma Master Kō of Kion-ji Temple, the five stages of abiding delusions (*pañca-vāsabhūmi-kleśa*) are all collectively the delusion of ignorance (*moha*). Furthermore, this has been traditionally transmitted from ancient times.
According to the purport of the *Yingluo jing*, the arhat’s merit is equal to that of the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*).

Regarding the seventh stage and above, the masters of the school maintain that the "afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges," the five kinds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and the nine grades of ignorance—namely, the nine grades of delusion—are all included therein.
As for the bodhisattvas of the thirty mental states (*triṃśac-cittotpāda*), they subdue the manifest afflictions; these may also be said to be "severed" by the power of the cause of retribution.

It is through the power of overcoming obstacles (*bādhana*) and the power of the cause of cultivation (*abhyāsa-hetu*) that [afflictions] are extinguished. Thus, the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:

"When one dwells in the stage of the Dharma of Patience (*kṣānti-dharma*), one severs the retribution of the three evil realms (*durgati*). One should know that this extinction does not arise from the conditions of wisdom (*jñāna-pratyaya*). Furthermore, there are differing interpretations regarding the meaning of "subduing" (*ava-sthāpana*).

First, some say it is like stacking grass (*tṛṇa-avasthāpana*). Second, others say it is like the overlapping scales of fish (*matsya-tanu-avasthāpana*). Third, the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra* (or *Baoen jing*) says: "Necessarily..."
One must understand that each category is mutually subsumed by the others. A Bodhisattva of the First Ground (*bhūmi*) eliminates the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) but does not subsume them;

however, in relation to the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*), there is also the sense of subsuming them. From the Second Ground up to the tenth Ground, Bodhisattvas both subsume and eliminate [the delusions].
A Bodhisattva at the stage of the Diamond-like Mind (*vajropama-citta*) subsumes them but does not eliminate them. At the stage of Buddhahood, they are eliminated but no longer subsumed.
Furthermore, if one distinguishes between wisdom (*jñāna*) and delusion (*moha*) in contrast to one another: from the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) downwards, it is as previously explained.

Regarding the four abodes of delusion (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), namely the delusions of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-kleśa*) and the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) within the three realms, which rely on the five [categories of] nine grades of ignorance (*ajñāna*):

for each of the four [abodes], the nine grades, and the three types, one respectively eliminates the obstruction of the path (*mārga-āvaraṇa*). Regarding the delusions that are severed or suppressed from the seventh stage upwards, there are likewise [distinctions].
There are three distinct natures: first, the nine grades of the universal delusion of the *avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi* (the ground of ignorance);

second, the nine grades of non-cognition (*ajñāna*); and third, the nine grades of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). These three natures are subsumed under one category: that which is severed and suppressed by the Path.

Furthermore, the five kinds of material atoms (*rūpa-paramāṇu*) in the world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are likewise included within these natures of ignorance, non-cognition, and habitual tendencies. For this reason, only these three types are established.

Regarding their nature, if categorized by name, there are four types. As for their abandonment and suppression: in the seventh stage, one abandons the afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and suppresses the ignorance regarding the objects of form (*rūpa-viṣaya-ajñāna*).
In the eighth stage, one correctly abandons the ignorance regarding the objects of form and suppresses the ignorance regarding the difficulty of the mind (*citta-durjñāna-ajñāna*).

In the ninth stage, one correctly abandons the ignorance regarding the difficulty of the mind and suppresses the ignorance regarding the arising of accumulation (*saṃudānana-ajñāna*). In the tenth stage, one correctly abandons the ignorance regarding the arising of accumulation...
The arising of "ignorance" (ajñāna) subdues the beginningless ignorance (*anādikālikāvidyā*). The remaining two types of aggregates are contained therein. Question:

Habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are the residual traces of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); how can they be equal in weight to the ignorance of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi-ajñāna*)?

He replied: "The [defilements] arising in ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who possess outflows (*sāsrava*) are still light; how could it be that the residual habits (*vāsanā-śeṣa*) remaining in the noble ones (*ārya*) of the Three Vehicles are heavy? Question:

According to the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* (Ten Stages Treatise), one has already severed the afflictions of the three realms (*tridhātu*) through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) at the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).

Why, then, does it say that they are only severed from the second and third stages onward? Answer: It is as when one says, "Because the cause is extinguished, the fruit is forgotten. This is a remote sense of subsuming the effect within the cause.
This clarifies that it is not a matter of categories or mutual opposition. Regarding the clarification of the Mahāyāna meaning:

there are those who, through the power of severing and subduing various types of afflictions, have from the time they were ordinary beings for immeasurable kalpas delighted their minds in the study of the sūtras and attained the Mahāyāna of non-attainment (*anupalambha*).

Or, within the provisional stages over countless kalpas, there are those who study non-attainment; among these, one person has washed their mind and intentions through the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). This is precisely...
As the Sūtra says: "The wisdom that accords with a single thought-moment cuts off immeasurable afflictions along with their habitual tendencies.
If this is so, why does it only mention the cutting off of the conceptualizations of the three realms? Now, the intention of the Mahāyāna anticipates both types of abandonment and suppression;

this is also stated as a secondary explanation within the sūtras and śāstras. However, because the underlying mental disposition remains, they ultimately do not depart from the tenets of annihilationism or eternalism; therefore, they are refuted.

Therefore, regarding the elucidation of the meaning of the Mahāyāna: for those whose faculties and conditions are inclined toward a single type of practice, or for those whose faculties and conditions delight in manifold merits, one may speak of "opening" [the path] as the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and the clarification of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
This refers to the severance [of afflictions] from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward.

However, for those with sharp faculties who have studied for immeasurable eons and realize non-attainment (*anupalabdhi*), it is not strictly necessary to open [the path] in two ways; thus, it is like the ascetic practices (*dhūta*) of a Bodhisattva.
It is said: "Those of the most superior faculties neither emerge from birth-and-death, nor do they enter into nirvāṇa. Furthermore, a sutra states:

"When I attain Buddhahood, there will be no names such as the Three Jewels," and so forth. Moreover, according to the sutras and śāstras, there are two ways of clarifying the meaning of "removal" (*apoha*):
first, clarifying it through the gate of merit, such as generosity overcoming stinginess, up to meditative concentration overcoming distraction; second, [clarifying it through the gate of wisdom].
This is elucidated through the gateway of wisdom: right view subdues false views, and even contemplating dependent origination can subdue delusion and the like.

Though non-dual, they are treated as dual; this is explained in terms of provisional designations applied to the provisional. Furthermore, from the perspective of the gateway of merit, one subdues the branches and twigs.

It does not mean that the fundamental delusions of appearance are not subdued. Within the gate of contemplation (*guanmen*), by practicing and studying emptiness and non-existence, one is able to subdue the fundamental [delusions], and the secondary branches are naturally forgotten; this is what is meant by "nameless marks" being spoken of as provisional names.

Furthermore, when the meaning is explained by dividing it into gates for the time being, the practice of the wisdom of emptiness can subdue the delusions of appearance; this must necessarily proceed in sequence from the heavy to the light, and there is no middle way.
The sequence here is not fixed, as in the meaning of the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), which proceeds from the shallow to the deep.

However, regarding the distinct knowledges and various meritorious practices within the Middle Way, these mental activities each arise with varying degrees of depth, such as when the practice of giving is already deep while the practice of meditative concentration is still shallow.
Alternatively, contemplating principle may be deep while contemplating phenomena remains shallow. This concludes the section on the gates of distinct practices.

Since the categories (kula) are not identical, the sprouts likewise arise differently. Furthermore, within the ranks themselves there are levels of depth and shallowness, ranging from the lower to the middle and up to the upper.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "There are superior, middling, and inferior; specifically, the lowest-of-the-low, the middling-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low."
Middle-low, middle-middle, middle-high; upper-low, upper-middle, and upper-high. Furthermore, as the Mahāyāna Sūtra says, it is like the analogies of uprooting trees and washing clothes.
The Sūtra states: "From the distracted mind one enters the first dhyāna; from the first dhyāna one enters the second dhyāna."

This continues until one enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Emerging from the absorption of cessation, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*);
emerging from that, one enters the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). In this manner, one successively descends through the lower stages to emerge in the distracted mind (*vikṣipta-citta*).

Such is the sequence of entry and emergence. Furthermore, the sūtras and śāstras state: from the distracted mind one enters the second dhyāna; from the second dhyāna one enters the fourth dhyāna; skipping these intermediate stages in succession, one thus enters the absorption of cessation.

Emerging from meditative absorption is likewise so. There are successive and alternating modes of emerging from and entering the cessation-attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*), as well as various modes of ascending and descending through it.
Since the practices of meditative absorption are thus manifold, the same applies to all other categories of practice. Although they are non-dual, they appear as dual;
when opened up, they unfold into immeasurable gateways like writing in the sky—leaving no trace, existing only as provisional names and designations.

[The text] says: There is no practice of emptiness that differs from the practice of existence; there is no practice of existence that differs from the practice of emptiness. There is no entry distinct from emergence; there is no emergence distinct from entry.

There is no difference between transcending and following, nor between transcending and not transcending, and so forth. This is because the two treatises—namely, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*—are subsumed within the same stage, as are the two schools of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.
Thus, there is a fixed locus. Those of sharp faculties encounter [this realization] through a single flower, a single blade of grass, a single color, a single fragrance, or a single light.
Illumination is precisely that which can sever and subdue immeasurable afflictions; even by smelling the fragrance of food, one may awaken to non-arising (*anutpāda*).

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Within the one, understand the immeasurable; within the immeasurable, understand the one. Thus they arise in mutual succession; this is truly the wisdom of the fearless.
Why must there necessarily be the gate of gradual progression (*anupūrva-mukha*) and the gates of leaping over or following the sequence? Furthermore, it is necessary...

One must skillfully discern the objects of cognition, the cognitions themselves, and so forth. However, when one transforms these objects and cognitions, the myriad dharmas possess no dual characteristics.
They are neither existent nor non-existent, yet not non-existent; they are ultimately pure. This is precisely the meaning of abandonment and suppression. Within this, there is ultimate purity.
This is termed the meaning of "severance. Within this, that which is obscure is termed "subduing. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"The wisdom corresponding to a single thought-moment severs immeasurable afflictions along with their habitual tendencies. Regarding the meaning of severance and subduing in the Mahāyāna of Non-attainment, one clarifies it through practice:
by reflecting back upon one's own mind, one finds that the mind is not a mind; it is ultimately pure, such that neither the four propositions nor the five propositions can be apprehended.
What afflictions are bound to the mind? What mind can be bound by afflictions? Therefore, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* says: "The mind, intellect, and consciousness have already ceased.
Thus, the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the Chapter on Characteristics and Practice, says: "One does not accept practice; one does not accept non-practice;
one does not accept both practice and non-practice; one does not accept neither practice nor non-practice; and one does not even accept non-acceptance."
"It is not received. The *Samantabhadra-paripṛcchā* (or *Sāramati-sūtra*) also says: "If the mind and mental factors do not function, one practices the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, that chapter says: "In this way, Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā*, it is like the walking of a person conjured by a Buddha.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* (or *Dhūta-piṭaka*) states: "The Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha questioned the Mind-King."
The Bodhisattva asked: "Regarding the observation of the nature of afflictions to deliver sentient beings within, its characteristics can be understood.
But as for external phenomena, how are they? Cittarāja Bodhisattva replied: "Internal and external phenomena are not different. Although they are not different, one must first observe the internal.
When a single affliction is purified, many are also purified. Why is this so? Because the internal is the root of the external and the source of all sages."
Having attained this wondrous Dharma, one uses the Dharma to deliver sentient beings. Sentient beings are inexhaustible; the Buddha-body is inexhaustible. Sentient beings are boundless;
the Buddha-body is likewise boundless. The nature of sentient beings is identical to the nature of empty space, and the nature of empty space is identical to the Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, that sutra states: "The mind is a venomous insect; the Mahāyāna Dharma is the staff. One whips the venomous insect of the mind within and without."
It is purity. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "To have no mind regarding self or other, yet to be able to fill all things.
Often the sūtras say: "There is no mind or intention. The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "It is like a conjured person preaching the Dharma for a conjured person."
One must not preach the Dharma while contradicting this intention. The "Chapter on Arising and Perishing" (*Nirvāṇa-parivarta*) in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"If there is any dharma that is grasped, it is all either eternalism or nihilism. Furthermore, various Mahāyāna sūtras frequently cite the example of a person created by illusion preaching the Dharma to reveal that the Sage is without mind.
Regarding the doctrinal tenets of the four schools—the Sarvāstivāda, the Sautrāntika, the Yogācāra, and the Madhyamaka—they are consistently... [text truncated]

One attains the practice of one who is like a magically conjured person. Why is this so? Because in treatises such as the *Bhūmi-saṃgraha*, both the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) are included;
whereas in treatises such as the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, only the six consciousnesses are included. Thus, it is not the same as a conjured person preaching the Dharma.

According to the intention of our own school, in a general and coarse analysis, one speaks of the manifestation of afflictions, their severance through understanding, and their accomplishment through delusion. However, if one analyzes it according to its actual function, it concerns the manifestation of...
One contemplates the mind as it arises and ceases; this mind is completely purified through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Thus, the mind that has already arisen is itself accomplished, or follows its own nature. This is not like the schools that hold to "attainment," who claim that although afflictions have departed, the substance of a pure mind remains until one reaches Buddhahood.
Therefore, those masters cite the *Bhāryāsūtra*, which says: "Inconceivable wisdom severs [afflictions]."

"The treasury of all afflictions (*sarvakleśakośa*). This passage proves that the mere understanding [of emptiness] severs delusion. Now, according to the Mahāyāna school, this principle also applies generally;

however, when discussed in essential terms, there are two objects—emptiness and existence—and the dual purification of wisdom regarding them is called "wisdom of emptiness" (*śūnyatājñāna*), which severs the treasury of all afflictions.
Therefore, in our own school’s doctrine, the provisional [wisdom] suppresses while the middle [wisdom] severs; the middle suppresses.

Regarding the conventional (*saṃvṛti*): both the conventional and the middle [truth] are severed; both the conventional and the middle are suppressed. It may also be said that there are cases where the understanding of the conventional suppresses it while the understanding of emptiness severs it, and cases where the understanding of emptiness severs it while the understanding of the conventional suppresses it; emptiness and existence are both severed, and emptiness and existence are both suppressed. When discussed in detail:

if the conventional, emptiness, and existence are severed or suppressed, the middle truth immediately deviates from severance and remains perpetually suppressed. Why is this so? Because the resolution of ignorance and the awakening to truth exclude one another, and this is precisely because of the conventional nature. And...
Regarding the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) discussed previously: they are, for the time being, an opening of the provisional characteristics within the Middle Way. Question:

As stated previously, if those of sharp faculties can achieve both severance (*prahāṇa*) and suppression (*vibhava*) even with a single flower or a single blade of grass, may it also be said that those in the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) and the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*) have achieved what is called "severance"?
Answer: This is clarified through the principle of "two yet non-dual. As the Sūtra says: "Bodhisattvas who have first resolved their minds [are equal to] the Buddhas of the three periods of time..."

Regarding the Buddhas: their initial arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) may also be described as "cutting off" and "subduing. This same process of cutting off and subduing applies to the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśaccitta*).

It is likewise so for all stages from the first ground (*prathamabhūmi*) upward. However, as for the initial arousal of the mind, it refers to the very beginning of turning toward and entering the ultimately non-dual mind (*advayacitta*) from the state of an ordinary person;

this is what is called "arousing the mind. As for "subduing the mind," it means to dismantle existence and non-existence, and to dismantle non-existence and non-non-existence—this is the process of bending, folding, and moving [the mind].
To transform [the mind] such that there is no leveling of the characteristics of existence and non-existence is called "subduing the mind.

To sever the mind such that it transcends existence and non-existence to reach ultimate purity, departing from the four propositions and the hundred negations, is called "severance. This intention precisely intends for the characteristics to be removed; because these two aspects are viewed in relation to one another, it is explained by means of the provisional.
If this is so, then entering non-duality as described above is called "arousing the bodhicitta," which involves a turning back [from duality].

The characteristics of subduing and eradicating are now clarified. That which is temporarily pacified but not yet completely purified is called "subduing the mind" (*vashīkaraṇa-citta*); that which is eternally purified is called "eradicating the mind" (*prahāṇa-citta*). Therefore, our school states:

although the general intent regarding eradication and subduing is as described above, within the sūtras and śāstras there are four designations discussed in terms of the mutual opposition between delusion and awakening.
For example, there are two types: the afflictions of the "correctly active" stage (*samyak-prayoga*) and those of the "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), as well as those of "reflection" (*vicāra*).

Regarding coarse afflictions and delusions: from the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) upward, up to the sixth stage (*ṣaṣṭhī-bhūmi*), one abandons the afflictions of the household of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vitarka-kleśa*) along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

From the seventh stage upward, up to the tenth stage, one abandons the two kinds of ignorance-delusions (*ajñāna-kleśa*). Thus, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) says: "The Bodhisattva of the sixth stage is not yet..."

Consider the afflictions of wisdom (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Furthermore, many sūtras and śāstras concerning the seventh stage state that it is called the "Far-Reaching Stage" (*dūraṃgamā bhūmi*) because one is far removed from the three realms.

The reason for this is that there are two types of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*): first, the views and afflictions of the active outflows (*paryavasthāna*); second, the views and afflictions of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
A master of the śāstras says: "Habitual tendencies are specifically ignorance; collectively, they are the delusion of ignorance. These constitute three categories of textual divisions.

The *sāṃyojana* (fetters) are light; therefore, they are removed by a single path of abandonment. Now, the present treatise does not hold this to be so. How could it be that ignorance is the same as the latencies (*vāsanā*) in being light?
Is the harsh speech of Śāriputra and others of the same category as sudden ignorance? [The author] asks the masters such as Kaishan and others:

regarding the worldly dharmas and the patience of the stage of the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatākṣānti*), do the final moments of the stage of the knowledge of the paths and the initial moment of the first bhūmi coexist as the resolution and the delusion?

They do not occur simultaneously, and their explanations differ. First, the old tradition of Kaishan (Kai-shan) says: "The arising of understanding and the cessation of delusion occur at the same time;

however, one speaks of 'the arising of understanding' and thus 'the cessation of delusion,' but one cannot say 'because of the cessation of delusion, there is the arising of understanding. This interpretation is the most feeble.

The superior-grade delusions regarding the truths must necessarily reside on the periphery of the worldly mind. If they were on the periphery of the mind that understands through patience (*kṣānti*) and clear knowledge (*vidyā*), then that mind would never be accompanied by superior-grade delusions;
how then could one say that at the moment understanding arises, it is the cessation of superior-grade delusions? How can you explain them as being simultaneous with clear knowledge?

Furthermore, regarding your statement concerning the language of "the extinction of delusion," it refers to the non-existence [of delusion] when it exists; ultimately, this is to say that where there is the eye, there is delusion.

Previously, you ridiculed the notion of "non-time," claiming it could not coexist with clear understanding. This is like the "Chapter on the Source" stating that ignorance is the ignorance severed by the Buddha’s axe.
This ignorance, being without category, can only be said to be associated with the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*);
it cannot be said to be associated with the Buddha-mind (*buddhacitta*). The diamond-like mind is the preceding thought-moment, while the Buddha-mind is the succeeding thought-moment;

how could they exist simultaneously? Therefore, the time when understanding arises is the very time when delusion ceases. This interpretation is utterly groundless. Since this principle is thus established, it serves to sever the final lingering [expectations].

The first stage (*bhūmi*) is to be understood by analogy with this critique. The *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* states: "The arising of knowledge and the cessation of afflictions cannot occur simultaneously;

one can only say that knowledge arises because the afflictions have ceased. If this is so, then while the afflictions cease at the time of the worldly dharma (*laukika-dharma*), knowledge arises at the subsequent moment of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe-dharmajñānakṣānti*).
Therefore, it cites the *Śāstra* (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*), which says: "When merit is about to arise, demerit ceases. Furthermore, [this is] correct...

This refers to the arising of the fruit due to the cessation of the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and so forth. This master’s position regarding those two schools is far superior to the previous interpretation;

yet, in the end, it does not escape the fault of being identical to the view that [the fruit] exists eternally. If, according to your interpretation, the defilement does not yet exist, how could it be extinguished beforehand?

If that were the case, there would be no need to eliminate this defilement through the Path, nor could it be eliminated through mutual opposition. The difficulties raised by Kumārajīva are indeed immeasurable. Now...

This means it is as previously explained. As the masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* say: "Whether simultaneous or non-simultaneous, the forgetting of dharmas and their realization are ultimately neither time nor non-time;

this is called 'severing and suppressing' (*prahāṇa-vinodana*). Where could there be a relationship between understanding and delusion such that one must distinguish between simultaneity and non-simultaneity?
Question: If this is so, do you not discuss simultaneity or the sequence of before and after at all? Answer: [As stated above, they are ultimately beyond such temporal categories.]
Non-dual yet dual; when opened, there are two aspects. First, according to the *Śāstra* (Shèlùn): "When merit is about to arise, sin is extinguished.
This means that because the names of delusion are extinguished, liberation arises; this is how the principle ought to be. Second, because liberation arises, delusion is extinguished.
For if liberation does not arise, delusion will not be extinguished. Nevertheless, if one seeks to dispel ignorance through the understanding of liberation, [it is as follows:]...

Within that which is devoid of names and marks, one speaks by means of provisional names and marks; this is clarified through the application of the provisional. Furthermore, in the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and other texts, there is a shared tenet of the "existence" (yu) gate:

that liberation (*vidyā*) is identical to delusion (*moha*). This must refer to what is currently manifesting. While previously it was held that the accomplishment of liberation cuts off the accomplished delusion, here it is held that manifesting liberation cuts off manifesting delusion;
thus, it likewise speaks of "manifesting liberation," excluding the sense of cutting off accomplished delusion. If, at the time of awakening to the Middle Way...
It is neither understanding nor delusion; yet it can also be said to be neither understanding nor delusion because one has fully realized that which is neither understanding nor delusion.

To say that this is the meaning of "the Middle is Identity" (*chū-soku*) is likewise correct. Question: Does this not contradict the four propositions previously mentioned, such as "the Middle and the Provisional are both severed"?
Answer: Those four propositions were clarified in order to refute the common tendency to assert unilaterally that "the True is severed while the Provisional is not."

It is because they are severed. If one were to open up the duality within non-duality, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep, provisionally clarifying them through the severance and suppression of their mutual characteristics.
However, if one clarifies them comprehensively, the four alternatives (*catuskoṭi*) are as previously stated. This meaning will be explained in detail later in the section on the *vajra-citta*.
Furthermore, the Master of the Treatise, Kāśyapa (Kai-sen), said: "Regarding the five stages of expedient means (*pañca-upāya*) and the thirty minds, [the object of] contemplation..."

The explanations regarding the object (*ālambana*) differ according to the chronological sequence [of the Master’s life]. When the Dharma Master was at Mount Dongshan, his explanation stated: "It takes as its object the principle of the provisional.

When he went forth to Yangzhou, he said: "It takes the true as its object; it is not called 'taking the provisional as its object. Finally, when he was approaching death, he definitively stated: "It is that which takes the principle of the provisional as its object. Why is this?

For the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, in the chapter on the Four Unhindered Knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisamvidaḥ*), states: "The outsider asks: What is the proximate dharma?"* *Note: The Sanskrit for "What is the proximate dharma" is *katama upaniṣad-dharmah*. The Chinese term "近法" (*jìn fǎ*) corresponds to this.*
This stage is known according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). The Master of the Treatise replies: "It is so in relation to the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*.

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Three Samādhis" in the treatise states: "That which is cultivated in common refers to the cultivation of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*; this is worldly samādhi, existing within the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*).
The noble, correct samādhi refers to entering the stage of the Dharma (*dharmāvasthā*), that is, from the stage of *kṣānti* and above. Therefore...
One knows that the five expedient means (*pañcopāya*) and the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) both take the realm of the provisional and the ultimate as their object.

This is because the provisional and ultimate truth is itself the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). If that school were to take the true realm as its object, then upon emerging from the object of the provisional and ultimate, their understanding would advance without interruption, yet they would not be subdued when regressing.
Why? Because their mental activity would be led [by the true realm]. However, if they take the provisional and ultimate truth as their object, then they can also achieve subdual.
Regarding the term "cessation" (*prahāṇa*): it is like the cessation of the sprout of karma due to its retributive cause. The meaning clarified here in the Mahāyāna is fully as explained previously.

One attains both cessation and suppression (*vibhava*) with respect to both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). It can also be said that one attains cessation and suppression regarding that which is neither ultimate nor conventional. This applies if one’s intention is pure.
What is there to be severed or suppressed? When one opens [the door] through the skillful means of provisional names, there is nothing that cannot be spoken of. The masters of old have said:

"The contemplation of phenomena according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) leads to an understanding by which one enters emptiness. When the understanding of emptiness manifests before one, it is called the contemplation of true phenomena (*bhūta-dharma*), and it is termed the 'understanding of emptiness.
If one emerges from existence by means of emptiness, it is called the contemplation of conventional truth. This is precisely...

This is called "the understanding of existence. Previously, if there were no guidance from the understanding of emptiness for the understanding of existence, the understanding of existence would immediately encounter objects and give rise to attachment.

If one emerges from emptiness into existence, the guidance of the understanding of emptiness prevents one from becoming attached to objects. Because one knows that the conventional truth consists of the three provisional designations and seven calamities, and thus remains in non-action, one does not give rise to attachment;
by casting aside the mundane and entering the true, this is the understanding of existence supporting the understanding of emptiness as one emerges from emptiness.

There is. That is to say, the understanding of emptiness guides the understanding of existence. The understanding of emptiness is precisely the wisdom of emptiness; the understanding of existence is precisely the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*).

In that school, the understanding of existence is ultimately distinct from the understanding of emptiness, and the understanding of emptiness is ultimately distinct from the understanding of existence.
If there is skillful means but no wisdom of reality, this skillful means is also bound. If there is emptiness but no skillful means, this emptiness is also bound. As it is said:

This is bondage. If that is so, how could it be capable of severing or subduing? Now, I say one must rely on the sūtras: first move [the mind] through concentration, and then extract [the afflictions] through wisdom.

Subduing occurs through the provisional name of causes and conditions; severing occurs through the causes and conditions of the provisional name. Therefore, first use the provisional to destroy the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and next use causes and conditions to destroy spontaneity (*svatantra*).
This is precisely fundamental purity; one must then cross over by means of the Middle Way and the provisional. Emptiness is...
There is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). This existence is the existence of emptiness. Arising is the arising of cessation; cessation is the cessation of arising.
If it is thus, then striking, churning, moving, and turning are what is called the "path of subduing. Emptiness is not an empty emptiness; existence is not an existent existence.

Arising and cessation are not cessation and arising; they are neither arising nor cessation, neither empty nor existent. This is precisely the method for severing delusions and first entering the Way.
This is the Dharma. Furthermore, according to one school, there are ten obstacles (*āvaraṇa*): the first stage (*bhūmi*) eliminates the obstacle of the ordinary person’s notion of a self;

the second stage eliminates the obstacle of the gate of the body as a sentient being; the third stage eliminates the obstacle of the marks of the darkness of ignorance; the fourth stage eliminates the obstacle of pride regarding the understanding of dharmas;

the fifth stage eliminates the obstacle of pride regarding the purity of one's own body; the sixth stage eliminates the obstacle of subtle afflictions (*kleśa*); the seventh stage eliminates the subtle... [text truncated].

The subtle accumulation of hindrances: on the eighth stage, one eliminates the hindrance of effort within the signless; on the ninth stage, one eliminates the hindrance of being unable to benefit all sentient beings;

and on the tenth stage, one eliminates the hindrance of lacking mastery over all dharmas. Regarding the ten stages in relation to the ten hindrances, it clarifies the elimination of twenty types of ignorance:
on the first stage, one eliminates the hindrance of the ordinary person’s mark of self, which is the elimination of two [types of ignorance].
There are two kinds of ignorance: first, the ignorance that obstructs all dharmas; second, the ignorance that moistens the three evil realms. Question:
For what reason does a Bodhisattva of the First Ground eliminate the obstruction of the ordinary person’s mark of self? Answer:

If it is a Bodhisattva at the final moment of the Path of Cultivation (mārga-jñatā), they still possess residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*). Thus, although there are two kinds of views of self, these are also termed the "self of birth" and the "self of dharmas."

Question: Is the emptiness of both phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*) the same as the Master’s intention? Answer: It is vastly different. In the Mahāyāna, the meaning of the two truths is that both are empty of persons.
Why? Because both truths are provisional. If one speaks of the emptiness of phenomena, this refers to the Middle Way, where the true Dharma itself is the emptiness of phenomena.
Upon ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to eliminate coarse habitual tendencies and, being free from the view of self, attains [realization].

Because the true arising of dharmas is the emptiness of both [self and phenomena], it is said that one enters the stage of the true sages by eliminating the habitual obstacles of the self-view of ordinary beings.

To explain this briefly: although the first bhūmi severs two kinds of ignorance and eliminates the obstacles of the self-view of ordinary beings, the actual severances and suppressions at the first bhūmi are truly immeasurable.
How, then, can it be said that it specifically severs two kinds of ignorance and eliminates the obstacles of the self-view of ordinary beings? This is...

This is merely a summary of one perspective. Question: For what reason does the first stage (*bhūmi*) sever the obstacle of the ordinary person’s mark of self (*pṛthagjana-ātma-nimitta-āvaraṇa*)? Answer:

At the final moment of the Path of Cultivation (*mārga-bīja*) prior to the stages, one comes to loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and rejoice in the bliss of *nirvāṇa*, thereby abandoning the faults of birth-and-death.

To further seek the bliss of liberation is due to the presence of the "breath of self" (ātman-vāyu). Because this breath of self is absent, one cultivates various practices such as dhyāna to establish the self in a favorable state;
yet because the subtle trace of the mark of self still persists, it is called the "self of the ordinary person" (pṛthagjana-ātman).

Upon the clear realization of the first bhūmi, this is severed and one immediately departs from the view of self, attaining the true contemplation of emptiness and non-self; this is then termed the stage of a true sage (ārya).
Another school says: "There exists this principle of emptiness and non-self as an object to be realized. Now, however, it is not so. Previously, before awakening, one still spoke of having a self;
now, having awakened, one does not see anything external, yet what is seen is called 'self. Therefore, it is said that there is no self.
How could there be a separate principle of non-self to be realized? What was previously seen as having a self is termed 'delusion'; now, having awakened—"
"I" and "non-self"—this is precisely what constitutes subduing. This is itself cessation; it is merely that subduing is designated as cessation.

Where else could one find a separate cessation or subduing? To clarify this according to the stages: at the final moment of the Path of Cultivation (mārgajñatā), one has not yet abandoned the five fears.

This is because the habitual tendency toward the conceit of a self has not yet been completely washed away, and thus fear persists. Now, having attained the wisdom of true emptiness and non-self in the first bhūmi, [one no longer fears].

Because one perceives that a self can be apprehended, one is free from the five fears; thus, such a person is called a true Bodhisattva. Question: From which sutra or śāstra do the ten obstacles mentioned previously derive?
Answer: They derive from the *Saṃtati-vimokṣa-sūtra*, which states: "One severs the mind of the twenty-two forms of ignorance."
The first stage eliminates two delusions, and so on up to the tenth stage, which eliminates twenty delusions. Since each stage eliminates two delusions, there are thus ten obstacles in total.

[The character "取" (qu) replaces "木" (mu) in the Song edition. The final two delusions are those eliminated during the stages of training (*śaikṣa*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The twenty-two delusions are all transcended by the ten stages.
As for the twenty-two delusions: the first is the delusion of conceptualizing sentient beings and phenomena (*dharma*).

1. Delusion regarding the afflictions of the two miserable realms; 2. Delusion regarding subtle transgressions of the precepts; 3. Delusion regarding the four types [of birth]; 4. Delusion regarding craving for sensual desires; 5.
Delusion regarding the lack of fulfillment in learning and retention; 6. Delusion regarding craving for meditative absorption (*samādhi*); 7. Delusion regarding craving for the Dharma; 8.

Delusion regarding the contemplation of turning away from *saṃsāra*; 9. Delusion regarding the contemplation of turning away from *nirvāṇa*; 10. Delusion regarding the arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); 11. Delusion regarding all conditioned phenomena...
13. Delusion regarding signs; 14. Delusion regarding subtle signs; 15. Delusion regarding skillful contemplation; 16. Delusion regarding the subtle arising [of phenomena];
17. Delusion regarding mastery over signs; 18. Delusion regarding the superior, superior knowledge of immeasurable *dhāraṇīs* and immeasurable syllables and phrases;
19. Delusion regarding eloquence (*pratibhāna*); 20. Delusion regarding supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); 21. Delusion regarding subtle secrets.
21. Ignorance regarding the subtle nature of the actual experience (*anubhava*) of the *āryajñāna*; 22. Ignorance regarding obstructions. The Master of Treatises (*śāstrakāra*) asks:

Since the five stages of expedient means (*upāya*) and the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) and so forth contain the delusions regarding the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of what is to be understood, why are they not designated as "conditioning true reality" (*tattvālambana*)?
"Now, is the Mahāyāna also explained in this same way? The answer is: "They are not all the same. Here, we shall simply set forth the differing explanations of various masters.

First, Nanjian says: "The delusive afflictions (*kleśa*) of the nine grades of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception enter into the substance of the semblance-understanding (*sādṛśya-adhimokṣa*).

However, because the ninth grade of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception consists of afflictions outside the [three] realms, the characteristic of the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) is an outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) outside the realms."
This is what is to be abandoned. Now, it is said that this intention does not belong to the school of the Lesser Meaning (Hīnayāna).
If that were so, there would be no sense of being "subsumed" within the essence of the first dharma-comprehension (*dharmajñānakṣānti*). Second, the *Zhuāngyán* (Ornament) states:

"Since the superior-grade delusions regarding characteristics (*nimitta*) associated with the vision of the truths have already been suppressed, the delusions regarding characteristics of the second grade and above all obtain the status of being subsumed within the essence of 'semblance-comprehension' (*anukūla-jñāna*). Third, the *Fǎyún Bào'ēn Lóng* (Dragon of the Dharma-Cloud Repayment of Kindness).

Guang transmits the interpretation of Kaishan as follows: "The delusions of the nine grades of non-characteristic (fei-xiang) are equal in their essential nature to the delusions of the five stages of expedient means (wǔ fāngbiàn) and the thirty minds (sānshí xīn).

If this were so, then the delusions of the essential nature and characteristics (ti-xiàng) in the first dharma of the path of immediate succession (wújiān dìyī fǎ) would be exactly equal to the delusions of the ninth grade of non-characteristic. Why? Because the delusions of the ninth grade of non-characteristic are the very beginning of the arising of characteristics."
The first characteristic of the Dharma is the culmination of the exhaustion of characteristics. At the beginning, one proceeds from the light toward the heavy;

at the end, one proceeds from the heavy toward the light. Therefore, these two stages are equal. This principle is evident in the teachings of the Hīnayāna; likewise, it applies to the categories of delusion and awakening in the teachings of the Mahāyāna.
However, the principle clarified in the Mahāyāna is not like this: there is no delusion through which one enters awakening, nor is there any awakening.

It contains delusion (*moha*). However, by means of provisional names and designations, it is opened up into "delusion" and "liberation" (*mokṣa*); these are the causes and conditions for delusion and liberation.

If one has not yet attained pure and complete awakening, it is called "containing delusion. When one has attained ultimate awakening, it is called "the characteristic of having exhausted delusion. Where else could there be a separate essence of liberation?
Since it contains the essence of the delusions of characteristics, why is it not weighed as a condition? Now, the school of Non-attainment clarifies this:
that wisdom and so forth are all ignorance; therefore, they must be washed away.
Second is the discussion of cultivation. Regarding the gate of cultivation, the masters of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* offer differing interpretations.

According to the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, there are ten stages of merit in the cultivation of hearing and practice. Within the thirty mental states (*citta*), the first ten mental states cultivate the merit of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Among those, the [next] ten mental states cultivate the merit of the second stage, and the final ten mental states cultivate the merit of the third stage. Within the first stage, one cultivates...
The virtues of the fourth stage: within the second stage, one cultivates the virtues of the fifth stage; within the third stage, one cultivates the virtues of the sixth stage;
within the fourth stage, one cultivates the virtues of the seventh stage; within the fifth stage, one cultivates the virtues of the eighth stage;
within the sixth stage, one cultivates the virtues of the ninth stage; and within the seventh stage, one cultivates the virtues of the tenth stage. This is...
To speak briefly in terms of the stages (*bhūmi*), they are generally arranged in this order, yet it is not entirely so. Why?

It is because the realization of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the essential requirement for accomplishing the stages. The merits one cultivates do not necessarily follow the sequential characteristics of the stages.

For example, one may have already cultivated the twelve gates of dhyāna prior to the stages, yet cultivate this specific method after the third stage; thus, it becomes a gate of non-fixed concentration (*aniyata-samādhi*). It is like this.
The same applies to other categories of practice. Now, I say this is not necessarily so. For instance, within the nine, eight, thirteen, and ten stages (*bhūmi*), why would one not cultivate merit?
If it is said that in every thought-moment one contemplates both emptiness and existence simultaneously, this is precisely the cultivation of merit and wisdom.

Why then must one insist on saying that within the five, six, seven, and three stages, one cultivates the merits of the nine, eight, ten, and [other] stages respectively? This is an opening [of the argument].
The virtuous disciple said: "The two paths of emptiness and existence advance together; however, only the path of existence possesses one additional grade.
Therefore, although the Bodhisattva of the Diamond Mind has practiced the myriad deeds of existence equal to those of a Buddha, he lacks the single grade of the wisdom of emptiness.

For this reason, he is called a 'Buddha of Equal Enlightenment' (Samyaksambuddha). Question: Regarding the afflictions subdued by the thirty mental states of the first stage Bodhisattva—what virtues eliminate them? What two [virtues]?
Question: The practice consists of only one category of conduct. Answer: That is because the teachings of the Hīnayāna do not clarify the meaning;

within the fifteen moments of mind, one does not emerge from contemplation. However, according to the meaning clarified by the Mahāyāna, within the initial stages of the *Gongpin* (Chapter on Merit), one emerges from contemplation to cultivate the ten thousand practices.

It is merely that the final [chapter] is one grade longer than the first. However, because it requires the profound merit to assist and trigger the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*), the chapters practiced therein are for the most part profound.

Now, the clarified meaning of the Mahāyāna possesses four permutations: there is the case where the understanding of existence (*bhava*) is extensive and deep, while the understanding of emptiness is superior yet shallow;

there is the case where the understanding of emptiness is extensive and deep, while the understanding of existence is small and shallow; and there is the case where the understanding of existence... [text ends].

There are variations in degree—more or less, shallow or deep—but in the realization of emptiness, there is no such distinction of degree or depth. For example, within one, one realizes the immeasurable;

within each measure of the immeasurable, one realizes the one. However, the realization of the immeasurable within the one and so forth is distinguished according to those who practice with effort and those who practice through emptiness.
I shall briefly clarify this according to the fundamental tenets of our school: there is the practice that accords with the cultivation of merit to bring forth the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If we discuss this in terms of various root-natures (*indriya*), there is no fixed rule regarding whether they are singular or multiple, provisional or real, or whether they enter or emerge from one another. As the Kaishan [Master] said:

"Because the practice of emptiness is long and profound, it is by this single grade that the ignorance-abiding ground (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) is severed by the Buddha’s wisdom of bodhi. This is as explained in the *Bhāryāsūtra* (The Scripture of the Consort).

Question: Regarding those who practice concentration equally with wisdom, there are three types of wisdom for the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna; does concentration likewise follow this pattern? Answer: This serves as a general rule.
For now, according to what the masters of the treatises say, there are three kinds of Śrāvakas: first, the "filling" Śrāvaka, which refers to one who fills both concentration and wisdom;
second, the "meaning" Śrāvaka, which refers to one who [attains] the meaning of concentration and wisdom; third, the "nominal" Śrāvaka, which refers to the nominal [designation].

Wisdom. Therefore, among śrāvakas, some attain the wisdom of the eight dhyānas while others do not. Third, the clarification of the meaning of attainment and non-attainment has two parts: (1) clarifying attainment and non-attainment;

(2) explaining simultaneous and non-simultaneous contemplation. Regarding the first, there are two points: (a) clarifying the stages of ordinary beings (pṛthagjana), both internal and external; (b) explaining the three types of regression.
Furthermore, the preceding treatise established the various stages and positions as provisional; however, that treatise also discusses attainment and non-attainment. As for the various stages...

The explanations differ. If one wishes to see [the teachings on] the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), the *Mūlakarma-sūtra* and the *Dharaṇīdhara-sūtra* clarify the meaning of the ten stages with particular clarity.
Furthermore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, the *Daśabhūmika-vyākhyāna*, the *Mūlakarma-avadāna-śiṣya-maṇi-sūtra*, the *Ratnarāja-sūtra*, and others all distinguish the ten stages.
As cited point by point in the *Great Meaning* (*Dà-yì*), they are now further clarified here. —Hùguó.

The third chapter of the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "There are the stages of the practicing lineage (*xi zhongxing*), the nature lineage (*xing zhongxing*), and the path-lineage (*dao zhongxing*) prior to the [ten] stages.

The *Yingluo jing* (Necklace Sūtra) states: "The first ten minds constitute the practicing lineage; the middle ten minds constitute the nature lineage; and the final ten minds constitute the path-lineage.
Furthermore, this sūtra says: "There are, moreover, six types of lineages. Which are they? The practicing lineage, the nature..."

The lineage (gotra), the lineage of the path (mārga-gotra), the noble lineage (ārya-gotra), the nature of equal enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi-gotra), and the nature of wondrous enlightenment (vibuddha-gotra).

The first three natures pertain to the stages prior to the [first] bhūmi; the latter three natures pertain to the stages from the first bhūmi onward. The *Dhāraṇī-śvara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that there are two types of abiding prior to the bhūmis:
first, abiding in the lineage; second, abiding in the stage of practice through understanding (adhimukti-caryā). Furthermore, it clarifies the lineage: "Briefly, there are two kinds. First..."

The first is the nature-seed-nature (*prakṛti-gotra*), and the second is the cultivated-seed-nature (*samudānīta-gotra*). Regarding this, the masters of the Dharma interpret the meaning of the text as follows:

from the ordinary person bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana-prthagjana*) upward, those who are naturally distinguished and superior are called the nature-seed-nature. Because their nature does not change, it is termed "nature."

When the cultivation of understanding has been perfected such that one no longer reverts to evil, this is called the *gotra* of the nature-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*). If it is attained through the practice of cultivation, it is called the *gotra* of the lineage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-gotra*).

Furthermore, it is not said that these two lineages differ in terms of superiority or inferiority. Moreover, the *Dharmadhātu-prakṛti-sūtra* analyzes the stages of practice into three types of patience (*kṣānti*):

namely, the lower patience corresponds to the first ten moments of mind; the middle patience corresponds to the middle ten moments of mind; and the upper patience corresponds to the final ten moments of mind.

It is the mind (*citta*). Furthermore, it is said that the stages of understanding and practice (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) constitute the initial arousal of the mind (*prathama-cittotpāda*), which has not yet reached the level of the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddha-citta-bhūmi*).
The Ground of Pure Mind is precisely the Ground of Joyful Contemplation (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Such is the classification of the stages according to the masters of the treatises (*śāstrakāra*).

Now, I say that within the mind of the initial arousal of the mind, there are three types of provisional arousal: first, that which is elucidated within the contemplation of the Two Truths; this is the universal practice of non-apprehension (*anupalambha-sarvagata*).

The Bodhisattva’s arousal of the mind consists of three aspects: first, it is the arousal of the mind through the six perfections; second, it is the arousal of the mind by possessing the contemplation of the Middle and the Provisional;

third, it is the arousal of the mind by penetrating the fifty stages of mind. Therefore, it is said that "understanding, practice, and abiding" constitute the arousal of the mind; however, this merely explains the initial arousal of the mind.

There are two meanings regarding the state of not yet having attained the Ground of Pure Mind (*śuddhabhūmi*). First, it refers to the initial arousal of the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*), which possesses the capacity for fulfillment and serves as the Ground of Pure Mind.

Second, it refers to the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśaccitta*) prior to attaining the joy of contemplation in the first ground; therefore, it is said that they have not yet reached the Ground of Pure Mind. As the *Dharanimdhara-sūtra* states:
"The two types of positions of practice through understanding (*adhimukticaryābhūmi*) are specifically termed the fifty minds; these are called the stage of practice through understanding."

This refers to all three stages. Question: What are the stages of the outer and inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*)? Answer: Regarding the classification of the stages, the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*—the two treatises of the Sarvāstivāda and Yogācāra schools—offer different explanations.

One view states that from the first six moments of mind downward constitutes the stage of the outer ordinary being, while from the seventh moment of mind upward constitutes the stage of the inner ordinary being;
thus, the *Ratnavali-sūtra* (瓔珞經) and the *Mūla-karma-saṃgraha-sūtra* (本業經) are cited as evidence, and both sūtras agree on this point.
It is said: Śāriputra fell back to the stage of a Hīnayāna practitioner during the sixth mental state (*citta*), but upon reaching the seventh, he no longer regressed;

therefore, regression is categorized as "external" and non-regression as "internal. Second, it is said that the first ten mental states constitute the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), while from the middle ten mental states upward constitutes the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*).
Thus, the *Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa-sūtra* (Pusa duanjie jing) states: "There are twelve types of noble persons (*āryapudgala*). It says:

The first ten mental states constitute those who practice by way of nature (*dharmatā-carita*); the latter ten mental states are called those who practice by way of understanding (*adhimukti-carita*).

Taking the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as ten persons, and combining these two groups, one obtains the twelve worthy ones (*dvādaśa-āryapudgala*). Since the Sūtras do not count the persons of the first ten mental states, it is known that they still belong to the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
Thirdly, many masters of the treatises generally state that all thirty mental states are internal ordinary persons (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*).

This stage is analogous to the five stages of the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) within the Small Vehicle. Therefore, in the *Dhāraṇī-śīla-sūtra*, it is said that among the forty-two noble beings (*āryapudgala*), the first ten mental states constitute the Stage of Cultivating the Seed-nature (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*);
the middle ten mental states constitute the Stage of the Innate Seed-nature (*prakṛti-bīja-gotra*); and the final ten mental states constitute the Stage of the Path-seed-nature (*mārga-bīja-gotra*).
Furthermore, adding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) to these preceding thirty mental states, the Vajra-mind constitutes the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samaya-bodhi-bhūmi*). This is the Buddha.

The Grounds (bhūmi) constitute the stage of wondrous enlightenment; thus, there are forty-two. Furthermore, the reason we know that the thirty minds (*triṃśaccitta*) precede the first ground is stated in the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "The thirty minds are all stages of skillful means prior to the grounds.

Moreover, within these stages, one is already able to extensively cultivate roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), practice various virtuous deeds, and skillfully train in the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), making offerings to all [Buddhas].

The Buddha practiced all pure and white dharmas and acted as a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) to protect [beings]. Being endowed with such a stage of the Dharma, there is no possibility of retrogression;

therefore, it should be known that this is the stage of the internal ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Furthermore, because one wears but a single robe among the four reliances (*catur-niśraya*), this is the stage of the internal ordinary person.

The stage of generating the mind through the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā-citta-utpāda*) is the external ordinary person. This is the meaning clarified in the Mahāyāna; as previously stated in the "Mountain Text" (*Shan zhong jiu yun*).
From the point of reversing the mind through the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one enters the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātma-prthagjana*) Bodhisattva.

Having already been able to manifest the eightfold path of enlightenment (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*), they act as teachers for devas and humans. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* and the final fascicle of the *Kāśyapa-parivarta* state in seven-word verses:
"The initial resolve and the ultimate [enlightenment] are not two different things; of these two minds, the former is more difficult. To seek to save others before one has saved oneself—"
Therefore, I pay homage to the initial generation of the bodhicitta. Once the mind has been generated, one becomes a teacher of devas and humans, surpassing both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Such a generation of the mind pervades the three realms; thus, it is also the primary basis for reliance. The "Chapter on the Threefold Wisdom" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* also states:
"From the initial generation of the mind, one practices this and that. Is this not indeed practicing this and that from the very beginning of generating the mind?

Question: The five expedient means (*pañca-upāya*) of the Hīnayāna constitute the stage of the internal ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). This is fully explained as it is set forth in the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*.

By analogy between the Great and Small Vehicles, one may follow what that master has taught. Answer: This is not comparable. Within the Hīnayāna, they cite teachings that are not definitive (*neyārtha*); how then can there be such an analogy?
Within the Hīnayāna, only those who attain the Way in a single lifetime (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*) may be compared; the Mahāyāna likewise attains [the Way] in a single lifetime.

Is it that one attains the Way through birth? According to the intent of the Mahāyāna, within the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one is already able to achieve the Way through the eight manifestations (*aṣṭākāra-abhisambodhi*) and has already realized the *prajñāpāramitā* of the True Dharma.

How could one still be reckoned as an ordinary person (*bālapṛthagjana*) outside the ranks? Now, according to the intention of this school, prior to the Ten Faiths, those who practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) in a partial manner have not yet attained the *prajñāpāramitā* of the True Dharma; they have only attained the two types of "non-practice" (*apravṛtti*).

Using *prajñā*, they become internal ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Like those who practice without activity (*apracāra*), they are identical to the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*) in that they also have nothing to attain (*anupalambha*).
Thus, they accord with the internal [realization] of the Two Vehicles. Therefore, the "Mahatva" chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"There were sixty bodhisattvas who, under five hundred buddhas, practiced the six *pāramitās* and fully performed the myriad practices; yet, because they lacked skillful means (*upāya*), they realized the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)."
Therefore, they cannot enter the stage of a bodhisattva. This is also as clarified in the "Chapter on Encouraging Study":
there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who practice the six pāramitās for immeasurable kalpas, yet do not enter the stage of a bodhisattva, nor do they enter the stage of a śrāvaka.
These individuals are all those at the level of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*). Question: If this is so, both chapters clarify that the bodhisattva has no [definitive] practice.
"Is it the attainment of a bodhisattva? The answer is: "It is also not the non-attainment of a bodhisattva. To set forth the underlying intent:
regarding the stage of that bodhisattva, when evaluated in accordance with the emptiness of the two truths, it is also considered an attainment;

therefore, as one still at the stage of an external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*), they are refuted—just like the bodhisattvas of the four schools such as the Di-shi (Dilun) and others. Now, it is said that prior to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), [it has not yet been attained].
Attaining the two truths as provisional, empty, and non-existent constitutes the stage of the external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).

Attaining the two truths as spontaneously empty, where existence is non-existence and there is nothing to be attained, constitutes the stage of the internal ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*). Therefore, the Master said:

"As long as one has not attained that emptiness, practicing with something to be attained is like the earth supporting the four classes of people. If one turns the mind and encounters a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who possesses the signs of non-attainment, one should focus [on this]."

To practice the conduct of non-attainment is like one who enters non-attainment; this is precisely how an outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) enters the inner ordinary person (adhyātmapṛthagjana).
Furthermore, by means of this outer ordinary person practicing non-attainment, they attain entry into the stage of non-attainment within the ten stages of faith (daśa-śraddhā).

Although they have entered the ten stages of faith, because they previously practiced through skillful means that were not yet direct, even though they have entered the correct position (samyaktva-niyāma), there still remains [the distinction of] clarity.

Because [the stages] are obscured, they are opened up into ten grounds (*bhūmi*). If one has not yet attained the state where the two truths are both empty and non-empty, then even if a person who practices "non-attainment" for immeasurable kalpas—such as those at the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*)—practices for immeasurable kalpas, for those of sharp faculties, there is the principle that they may suddenly sever all delusions and wash them away completely.
