twelfth is the stage of relinquishing the Lesser Vehicle and turning toward the Great Vehicle; thirteenth is the tenfold dedication of the Great Vehicle.

The stages directed toward the ground: fourteenth, the ten grounds; fifteenth, the Buddha-ground; the marks, wisdom, and merit of the Tathāgata; sixteenth, the stage of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa with remainder);
seventeenth, *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa without remainder). These two nirvāṇas constitute the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa*).
Now, it is said that this is neither with remainder nor without remainder, and it is neither wisdom nor cessation; it is merely given the provisional name "nirvāṇa without remainder."
Section Three: Clarifying the Time Periods and Kalpas.
According to the sutras, it is explained that there are three kalpas. Regarding the ten *li* stone (some say a square stone forty *li* on each side):

using the garments of the gods of the six heavens of the desire realm, one brushes this stone once every three years by human reckoning of days and months. When the stone is worn away, that constitutes one small kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Six.
The Stone of Ten Li: The robes of the Brahmā gods weigh six times as much as those of others. Every three years, they descend once to sweep the stone until it is worn away;

this constitutes one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). Yet, that heaven has neither sun nor moon; they determine the passage of years by means of the radiance of precious jewels, using *kai-ming* (opening-jewel) pearls to distinguish the number of years.
The Stone of Eighty Li: The robes of the Śuddhāvāsa gods weigh no more than two layers. They likewise descend once every three years to sweep [the stone] before...
When the stone is exhausted—if this constitutes one great kalpa—there would likewise be no sun or moon.
One might take the brilliance of a mirror to provide illumination for ease of understanding, thereby calculating the months and years within it. However, the duration of a kalpa is also not fixed;

some say that if a square stone eight thousand *li* or eighty thousand *li* in size were used, and one stone were removed every ten thousand one thousand *li*, then that would constitute a great kalpa.

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Incalculable Numbers" (*Asaṃkhyeya-parivarta*), states: To briefly summarize the essential enumeration, ten million is designated as one hundred million (*koṭi*);
ten million is one hundred million; ten million is one hundred million; ten thousand million *nayuta*s is one *gaṇana*;
ten thousand million *gaṇana*s is one *vibhava*; ten thousand million *vibhava*s is... [and so forth].
One *asaṃkhyeya*. *Saṃkhyeya* here means "incalculable," which is to say it cannot be described and cannot be measured. The various Dharma masters say:
if a stone ten thousand *li* in size were to last for a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*), that would constitute one *asaṃkhyeya*.

Now, to clarify this great kalpa in relation to the stages (*bhūmi*), distinguishing the duration and the relative fewness or manyness of the practice performed: it begins from the arousal of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
One makes mental offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the River Sītā for one kalpa, thereby attaining the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*).

With these ten stages of faith, after two kalpas, one reaches the beginning of the stage of the cultivated nature (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*). From this stage of the cultivated nature, by practicing for three kalpas, one attains the stage of the wisdom-nature (*prajñā-gotra*).

Due to the nature of the lineage (*gotra*), one attains the nature of the path (*mārga-gotra*) after four *kalpas*. The nature of the path lasts for five *kalpas*, after which one attains the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The first stage lasts for six *kalpas*, after which one attains the second stage. The second stage lasts for seven *kalpas*, after which one attains the third stage.
Having spent eight kalpas on the third bhūmi, one attains the fourth bhūmi. Having spent nine kalpas on the fourth bhūmi, one attains the fifth bhūmi.
Having spent ten kalpas on the fifth bhūmi, one attains the sixth bhūmi. Having spent eleven kalpas on the sixth bhūmi, one attains the seventh bhūmi.

Having spent twelve kalpas on the seventh bhūmi, one attains the eighth bhūmi. Having spent thirteen kalpas on the eighth bhūmi, one attains the ninth bhūmi. Having spent [thirteen kalpas] on the ninth bhūmi...

After ten thousand kalpas, one attains the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*). The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states that one studies the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of the Buddha for a hundred kalpas to reach the stage of Buddhahood.
According to the *Benye yingluo jing*, these combined periods total eleven thousand eight hundred and forty kalpas.
Only by practicing stage by stage can one reach the ground of Buddhahood. If one were like those of the Two Vehicles, it would take eighty thousand kalpas to reach ten thousand kalpas;

that is, through practice, one reaches the middle stage of the Ten Faiths. According to the *Renwang jing*, this calculates the number of intermediate kalpas from the stages prior to the grounds up to the attainment of Buddhahood.

Generally speaking, this is similar to the final summary which states that from beginning to end, one passes through immeasurable kalpas; however, this calculation begins specifically from the Ten Grounds.

"Reaching the Vajra-mind and reaching Buddhahood"—if one were to provide an explanation for this, it would not differ by even a hair's breadth from the *Benye jing* (Sutra on Original Karma). If one were to interpret it:

The various Dharma masters say: The *Benye jing* (Sūtra on the Original Vows) relies upon great kalpas (*mahākalpa*) for its exposition, while the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) takes middle kalpas (*antarakalpa*) as its basis;

thus, the textual passages of these two sūtras do not contradict one another. Furthermore, according to the *Zhuangyan lengqie zang jing* (Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-alaṃkāra), within each and every stage (*bhūmi*), one must pass through hundreds of thousands of great kalpas before the gateway to that stage is perfected; this does not take into account those of dull faculties.
Furthermore, if one clings to specific times and seasons, one does not serve the practice of stabilization.

Regarding the meaning of the *vajra*-mind, there are four sections: (first, clarifying the general intent; second, explaining the name; third, identifying its essence; fourth, analyzing and distinguishing it).
The first general meaning: The "vajra-mind" elucidated in the sutras and treatises is a metaphorical designation used to illustrate two types of phenomena:
the phenomenal (shi) and the noumenal (li). Why is this? First, it serves as a metaphor for the stage of ultimate study, which is equivalent to the various forms of learning.
The second is to use this as an analogy for the Way of Non-duality (*advaya*). These two meanings open up the fundamental principles of the horizontal and vertical [dimensions].
Only by possessing both the Middle and the Provisional can one truly weigh the Vajra; that which lacks the Middle and the Provisional is not the Vajra.
The term *vajra* has many meanings; in brief, it possesses two capacities: firmness and sharpness.
First, because the substance of the sublime jewel *vajra* is firm, it cannot be harmed by any object. Second, because it is capable of being sharp, whatever it is aimed at is shattered;
there is nothing it cannot break. Since the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is the *vajra* that is far removed from all states of going and not-going, it is compared [to this].
It is "solid" because it thoroughly dispels right and wrong; thus, it is likened to that which is indestructible, which constitutes its "sharpness.

Furthermore, at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), all accumulated defilements are exhausted; hence it is said to be "indestructible" and "sharp. That which no one can infringe upon is "solid."
Therefore, it is called the "Vajra-mind. Just as the wondrous jewel *vajra* is characterized by sharp utility and a solid essence, so too is this second explanation of its name:

"Vajra-mind" takes firmness and sharpness as its meaning. Because the Path of the True Dharma cannot be subverted by the hundredfold "non-is-nesses" (negations) nor can it be invalidated by the hundredfold "is-nesses" (affirmations), it is said that its meaning is "firm and substantial. Since there is nothing it cannot shatter when directed toward it, it is said to be "sharp."

"Principle" (*yi*) refers to the superior body of a Bodhisattva on the ten stages who possesses ultimate patience; because there is nothing it cannot penetrate, its meaning is "firmness" and "sharpness.
Regarding "mind" (*xin*), there are two senses: first, the true path as mind, as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*";
second, the mind that desires to cultivate the dharmas of the mind, which is not some remote object—the mind itself is [the locus].
Because it is the master of both delusion and awakening, when the spiritual intelligence (*śrāman*) of sentient beings refines their practice, they awaken to the fact that this mind is no-mind.
It is the gateway for entering into principle, and it is also the mind that attains the fruit; therefore, it is called the "Vajra Mind."
Third, the clarification of the essential nature (*svabhāva*). The Vajra-mind is of two kinds: first, the True Dharma as its essence;

second, if we discuss it crosswise, at the stage of ultimate study, when this [mind] illuminates the perfection [of reality], all burdens are completely exhausted. Its essence consists of both the dual interpretations of emptiness and existence.
Within these two functions, one may also say that the interpretation of permanence is primary. If one speaks in terms of looking toward the steadfast and correct path...

Thus, both dharmas are equally provisional functions and not the essence. Question: What is the stage of the essence of the diamond-mind (*vajracitta*)? Answer: There are differing interpretations. One says it is the limit of the stage of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*).

Regarding this "limit of the stage of training," there are also different explanations. One says that because it reaches the limit of training in relation to the fetters (*saṃyojana*), it is called "diamond.
As for the expression "stage of the essence," it receives the name "stage of the essence of the diamond" by way of reaching the ultimate limit of its functional activity. Therefore...
The "Vajra-jeweled vase" (vajra-bhājana) signifies being complete and without deficiency. The *Sanjian chuyi* states: "Taking cause and effect together constitutes the vajra-body.
This intention derives from the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which cites what was attained through emptiness under Dīpaṃkara Buddha; this serves as proof for the preceding [cause].
They consider it to be the *Vajra* stage based on that sūtra. The text states: "At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was no bodhi to be attained.
This proves that the state prior to attaining the fruit is the *Vajra* stage. Those masters and others, having fixed the locations of cause and effect, have made this statement.
Now, I say: although they are non-dual, they are discussed as two. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* is not a teaching for the Śrāvaka vehicle, nor is it...

The Buddha-dharma is the cause, which is named *prajñā*; the fruit is *bodhisattva-prajñā*. If one speaks of the *bodhisattva-prajñā*, then *prajñā* is the cause and *bodhisattva-prajñā* is the fruit.
Furthermore, if one refers to the three illuminations (*tri-avabhāsa*) mentioned in a fragment of an ancient great sūtra as *nirvāṇa*:
Regarding the stage of the fruition of the penetration of *prajñā*, if one discusses the True Dharma, *prajñā*—being like a great mass of fire—is neither cause nor fruit.
The "Vajra-mind" (*vajracitta*) specifically refers to the cause; it is designated as the Vajra-mind because it is the cause.
The fourth section: A clarification. Question: It was previously stated that "Vajracitta" refers to Vajrasattva;
however, *vajra* has many meanings. What are these multiple meanings, and what is their essential summary? Answer:
First, in the worldly sense, *vajra* means "purity," because it is free from defilement. Second, it means "supreme excellence," because it is the most excellent among all jewels. Third...
1. Its meaning is "difficult to fathom," because no one in the entire world is able to determine its fundamental value.
2. Its meaning is "difficult to obtain," because it is like a diamond in the world that a poor person cannot acquire. 3.

Its meaning is "possessing power," because it is like the precious wheel-treasure of a universal monarch (cakravartin) that flies through the air with sovereign ease, possessing great power and majesty. 4. Its meaning is "indeterminate."
If a vajra is placed among various colors, it changes according to those colors and lacks a fixed nature; this is the seventh meaning, "being the master.
For example, the precious wheel of a universal monarch (cakravartin) is the master of all jewels, and all other jewels follow it.
The eighth is the meaning of "being able to gather. For example, regarding the worldly vajra, if one obtains it, all precious objects are gathered at will.

The Collection of Teachings. Ninth, the meaning is "adornment" (*vyūha*) as the adornment of the teaching. Just as a diamond (*vajra*) can adorn a teaching, the Buddha is the head of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

These nine kinds of meanings are illustrated by the function of the diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), as explained in detail in the sixth chapter on the "Virtues of the King of Virtue" (*Guṇarājaparivarta*) in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*. Question: In the world, diamonds consist only of goat horn and tortoise shell.
There are two kinds of things that can cause injury or destruction. Now, regarding these two types of vajras—horizontal and vertical—is there not also a sense of "non-vajra"?
Answer: There are two kinds of worldly vajras: those that can cause injury or destruction, and those which no other object whatsoever can injure or destroy.
These also have two meanings: first, the partial sense, wherein other objects lack the capacity for injury or destruction; second, the ultimate sense of the vajra-mind through exhaustive study.
No afflictions can burden it; it is likened to that which merely arises and perishes. How much more so for the two kinds of entities?

Now, because the Way of the True Dharma is far removed from all things, and because all attainments and inversions are washed away within right contemplation, it is therefore termed "Vajra" (the Diamond).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the means of severing and that which is severed are not the same. One explanation states:
Both the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped) are discussed entirely within the context of conventional continuity; they do not exist within the realm of ultimate dharmas.
We know this to be so because when a single moment arises, it either passes away of its own accord and does not continue further, and is thus empty, non-existent, and so forth.
How, then, could there be a definitive "ability" to act as an obscuration? Therefore, it must be a continuous, uninterrupted process that has the capacity to produce the darkness of obscuration.

Using this principle as a basis for inference, it follows that the "proclivities" (anuśaya) which are abandoned must be understood in terms of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), and the "wisdom" (*jñāna*) that abandons them is likewise understood in terms of the continuum.
In terms of ultimate dharmas (*dravyadharma*), there is no such thing as a power capable of extinguishing [them].
Second, regarding the "occasional" (or) arising from factors that contradict the principle of liberation: if this occurs, how can one say that one [aspect] contradicts while the other does not?

The "occasional" that is to be severed is fundamentally established through contact; it is not called a provisional manifestation. The *Longguang* (Dragon Light) tradition transmits the doctrine of Kaishan:
it establishes a long-lasting provisional state lacking wisdom. Because there is a moment-to-moment cessation and extinction, it is not based on reality.

This is a discourse on the Dharma. Regarding the three explanations of the *Enzhuan*, it says: "According to the provisional discussion, that which is real is capable of severing; this is the understanding [of the subject]. That which is both provisional and real is that which is capable of being severed;

this is the doubt [of the object]. However, while the provisional exists, the real does not. The case of a sword severing grass and trees is not analogous. Why? Because the sword’s severing of wood and such is a phenomenon of form (*rūpa-dharma*);
thus, the seer and the seen, as well as the seer and the severed, are both provisional and real. Furthermore, it is said: "A sword severs wood and so forth..."

Since there is no actual accomplishment, it is explained through conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Because the real dharma (*dharmatā*) is sovereign, it does not depend on discourse regarding that which cuts and that which is cut.
To understand the nature of cutting is simply to realize that nothing exists; moment by moment, there is arising and ceasing, which is merely a state of flux and impermanence.
However, the meaning clarified in the Mahāyāna is not thus. As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra*, when one investigates and scrutinizes the self:

Regarding "what belongs to a self" (*ātmīya*): having realized that neither a self nor what belongs to a self can be apprehended, at that time, even if afflictions (*kleśa*) are still present within the scope of reality, they may still be termed "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*) or "suppressed" (*vibhāvita*).

This is not like the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and other treatises, which distinguish between the provisional and the real, asserting that abandonment and suppression consist in the cessation of their characteristics.

Question: The "Chapter on Distinctions" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The Bodhisattva practices the path of the unimpeded path (*ānantarya-mārga*) of abandonment; the Buddha [resides] in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). [What is the meaning of this?]
The Practice of the Path. What are the characteristics of these two practices? Answer: They are explained as two while being non-dual. The adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) is the cause;

the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*) is the fruit. The cause is unimpeded (*anāvaraṇa*); the fruit is liberation (*vimukti*). Thus they are named. The Master of Treatises could not grasp this unity. Nanjian Xian explained it thus:
when the meaning is raised, there is no distinction between the unimpeded and liberation; yet when cause and fruit are distinguished, the adamantine mind is the essence itself.

Unimpeded. The essence of the Buddha-fruit is itself liberation. Why? In the "Chapter on the Source of Subduing the Golden Mind," it is said that whether it be the essence, the decisive factor, or the power of the habitual fruit that draws [the result], the power of the cause for the release from hindrances directly constitutes this accomplishment.

Since the essence of the [Buddha-]stage exists, once these three powers are lost, there is no decision regarding the habitual fruit that draws [the result], and thus there is an obstruction. Therefore, the meaning of being unimpeded is revealed. Thus.

The "Eye" is the Golden Mind (*suvarṇacitta*). It is unimpeded. Since it already possesses the essence of potentiality (*bīja*), it is not insufficient to weigh against liberation. The meaning of liberation is non-obstruction.
Because it does not obstruct the Golden Mind, the causal habituation of the Golden Mind draws forth the fruit of Buddhahood;

by severing the source of these afflictions (*kleśa*) and their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), one becomes serenely unimpeded. Thus, the meaning of liberation is revealed, and it is called "liberation. Second, the Dragon Light.
Master Chao’s transmission of the teachings of Kaishan states: "The two paths of non-obstruction (*asanga*) and liberation (*vimukti*) are both names for the essence of the stage of fruition.
Why? Because the Buddha-fruit is the cessation of afflictions; thus, it is 'non-obstructive' in that it does not obstruct liberation, which is why it is called 'non-obstruction.

The essence of liberation is serene and free from entanglement, which is why it is called 'liberation. It is because of liberation that there is non-obstruction; it is not because of non-obstruction that there is liberation."

Liberation (*vimukti*) is superior to non-obstruction (*anāvaraṇa*), while non-obstruction is inferior to liberation. Therefore, liberation resides in the fruit, whereas non-obstruction resides in the cause.
Why? For instance, it is because one is bound that there is obstruction; one cannot say that because there is obstruction, one is bound.

Because it is liberation, it is unimpeded. This is clarified in the Mahāyāna school. To discuss it horizontally from the perspective of conventional designation, it is as explained by the Master Xian; it is also well-suited to clarify this within the context of names and words.

However, in that place, one falls into the Mahāyāna intent of "non-attainment," wherein merely realizing that this mind of existence and non-existence is ultimately exhausted is what is called "liberation.

This mind of existence and non-existence— *Note: The original text appears to be a commentary on the nature of liberation and the pitfalls of conceptualizing it through the lens of "existence" and "non-existence. The final sentence is left incomplete in the source.*
It is that which is bound. If this is so, the non-arising of the mental substance of existence and non-existence is called the Path of Non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Its ultimate exhaustion and liberation is called the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Since its meaning is opened up as "existence," the Sūtra states that what is non-dual is spoken of as dual:
"The Bodhisattva acts with non-obstruction; the Buddha acts within liberation. This is the meaning of cause and effect. By means of cause and effect, and by means of the effect...
Cause is the cause of the effect; effect is the effect of the cause. Therefore, there is no real cause within the effect, and no real effect within the cause.

Thus, within name and appearance, these two are opened up as non-existent, and thus there is no locus. Furthermore, it is like the provisional; therefore, within the middle there is no provisional, and within the real there is no middle.
As the *Shih-lun* (Treatise on the Ten) says: "Both provisional and middle—these two are likewise so. Question: Regarding non-existence...
Question: Are there lateral and primary [distinctions] regarding the hindrances and liberation? Answer: They are not two, yet they are two; this is clarified by way of their respective objects.

Both types are correct. If one were to distinguish them further: taking the hindrances as the primary, liberation would be lateral; taking liberation as the primary, the absence of hindrance would be lateral.
If it is said that within correct practice there is nothing to be attained, yet liberation from attainment is called "unhindered" and called "liberation," then such a thing does not exist.
The Auxiliary and the Principal. If one enters the Middle Way from the conventional, the conventional serves as the means of subduing [afflictions] and is also characterized by non-obstruction.
For the Bodhisattva, this is termed "severance" when viewing the Middle Way correctly; it is also the path of liberation, for it is the Buddha-way.

As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, thirteen fascicles, in the "Chapter on a Single Thought-Moment," states: "Non-apprehension is itself the Path, itself the Fruit, and itself Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, the *Bodhisattva Tóujīng* (The Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Head) states:

"When a bodhisattva first resolves upon the aspiration for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), they immediately attain perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) without proceeding through successive stages such as Equal Awakening (*samanvāgama-bodhi*) or Sublime Awakening (*miao-jue*). The preceding thought serves as the cause and the succeeding thought serves as the fruit;

this is the ultimate fruit within *nirvāṇa*, wherein the adamantine holy body and the seed-knowledge manifest before one. [The text] asks the Buddha: [Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "問佛" (Asks the Buddha). The translation reflects the available portion.]

When the fruits [of the path] are being abandoned or extinguished, that is precisely the time of Buddhahood. If this is so, does understanding arise at the time when those [fruits] are being extinguished?
The masters of the *Abhidharmakośa* (Cheng lun) offer differing explanations regarding this, as stated in the section on the meaning of the Ten Stages (*Daśabhūmi*).

One view holds that at the time of understanding, one is attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, while at the time the fruits to be abandoned are being extinguished, one is at the stage of the "Golden Mind" (*suvarṇacitta*). Since there is no distinction made between the fruit of Buddhahood and the Golden Mind, how can it be said...?
Is it at the time of arising or at the time of cessation? The gold must necessarily manifest as another Buddha; yet the gold-mind has already been suppressed and either exists or does not exist.

Since it does not obstruct the gold-mind among these three states, it draws forth the fruit of habituation (*vāsanā-phala*). When the fruit of habituation arises, the substance of the [gold] itself vanishes of its own accord.

At the time of this spontaneous vanishing, it is ultimately the time of the gold-mind; it does not reach Buddhahood. This meaning has already been [discussed] within the context of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
The refutation is concluded. Second, Longguang (Nāgaprabha) recounted the view of Kaishan (Kaiśana): "The time when liberation arises is the same as the time when [the obstacle] perishes.

For example, at the time of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*), it is the time when liberation arises and the [obstacle] perishes. Why? If the limit of patience is accomplished, its essence tends toward non-existence;

the patience toward suffering tends toward existence. Tending toward existence and tending toward non-existence are not sequential; therefore, they are said to be simultaneous. This is the source for the severance of the Buddha-fruit.

Regarding the "defilements of the categories": the manner in which these are severed and suppressed differs from other locations. Why is this? Because the source-category of ignorance culminates in being bound to the ignorance within the *suvarṇa-citta* (Golden Mind);
its essence ultimately does not depend upon the fruit of Buddhahood. Yet it is said that the wisdom of *bodhi* severs this ignorance whose essence has existed since beginningless time.
This is because if [the fruit] arises, the cause is extinguished; if it were not to arise, the cause would not be extinguished. For this reason...

The fruit must arise; therefore, the cause ceases. Question: If the arising fruit can sever the afflictions of the *kanjin* (golden mind), then would it not follow that there is a pre-existing affliction within the *kanjin* that is severed by a non-existent, quiescent attainment and a non-existent realization of the essence? Answer:

Because the fruit is about to come into existence, the afflictions on the side of the *kanjin* cease. If the Buddha-fruit were not about to come into existence, the afflictions would remain fully established within the *kanjin*.

Ultimately, there is no cessation [of the afflictions] through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) directed toward the fruit of Buddhahood, for they may instead be eliminated through the path of insight (*darśana-mārga*).

Therefore, one should posit that ignorance (*avidyā*)—the root category—is severed by the fruit of Buddhahood. Although this root category is associated with the Golden Mind (*suvarṇa-citta*), the Golden Mind is not its specific antidote;
thus, it is posited as being severed by the fruit of Buddhahood. Now, the meaning clarified in the Mahāyāna differs from these two views: [in some cases] the essence is originally...
It is not born; now it is also not extinguished. Understanding is likewise so. When wholesome words arise, perhaps understanding is extinguished and understanding arises;

or perhaps understanding arises and is extinguished. To harbor such shifting thoughts is itself a delusion. How could this possibly separate the ordinary from the holy? "The Holy" is merely a provisional name;

it is opened up as "understanding" or "clarity," and spoken of as "clarity" when one speaks of the method for attaining clarity. As stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "When merit is about to arise and evil is about to be extinguished, one attains..."

It is said that "either delusion ceases or understanding arises," yet constant understanding is itself what is deluded. Therefore, when delusion ceases, there is nothing lost; when understanding arises, there is nothing produced.

Ultimately traceless, this is called "severing and subduing. This is clarified at the stage of contact (*sparśa*), as it speaks of the Bodhisattva’s practice of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
thus, it is at the "Golden Mind" (*suvarṇacitta*) that delusions are severed. Question: The Sūtra says "Gold... [text truncated].

The characteristics of the mental factors (caitta) are as previously described in the "Moon in the Center" [chapter]. Because all afflictions (kleśa) are like smoke and subtle obstructions, the gold-like mind (*suvarṇacitta*) has not yet reached its ultimate exhaustion.

Answer: The intent of this sutra is that for a Bodhisattva with a gold-like mind, the afflictions have been exhausted like smoke and subtle obstructions, or perhaps they do not reach the state of a Buddha.
Question: Regarding the Bodhisattva with a gold-like mind, there are certainly two interpretations, both of which fall short [of the full realization].

"Is it the Buddha? [The questioner asks. The Master replies: "Generally speaking, when one discusses the level of understanding, there is a distinction between being equal to the Buddha and falling short of the Buddha by even a single grade.

Therefore, although those with the Vajra-mind are called 'Equal Enlightenment' (Samyaksaṃbodhi) Buddhas, if one were to discuss them according to their actual capacity, there would be differences in both their understanding and their clarity."
What is meant by this? Although the Golden Mind (suvarṇacitta) attains the rank of "My Own Category" (wú pǐn jīn xīn), it still involves the presence of doubt;
therefore, there is a lack of understanding regarding the Buddha-ground (buddhabhūmi). Because the Buddha-ground is free from doubt, it is luminous. Question:

If the understanding of the Golden Mind and the understanding of the Buddha-way are equal, are there no differences in depth between these two stages? Answer: There are differing interpretations. First, Master Nanjian Xian says: "Regarding the objective realm..."
There is a sense of relative shallowness and depth. Therefore, between the two wisdoms of *miao-jue* (wondrous enlightenment) and *deng-jue* (equal enlightenment), there is a sense of shallowness.
*Deng-jue* merely suppresses [afflictions] but does not sever them; it is only upon reaching the ultimate limit of manifestation that one attains equality with the Buddha.

Since the distinction between shallow and deep is difficult to discern, one must eliminate delusions before one can perceive the profound state. Furthermore, because [the latter] still carries the taint of impermanence, only the Buddha reaches the ultimate limit. Thus he answered him.

The former [masters] say that it may be a single stage (*ekabhūmi*), because within the objective realm itself there are naturally difficulties and ease. Master Chang of the Second Dragon [School] says:
"If explained according to the presence of understanding, then generally speaking, there is neither difficulty nor ease, for it is of one and the same grade of shallowness and depth.

Regarding the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*), it is said that his essence possesses two powers: first, the essence can obstruct understanding; second, the essence has ceased its function as an obstruction.
Since its function has already been subdued, there is no longer any power to exert force toward the fruit of its activity; it is like a dead person who is incapable of acting.
This is because one may look toward the auxiliary conditions for liberation, or because although the substance exists, it cannot cause liberation.
Since the illumination of liberation is partial and lacks non-duality, it fails to reach clarity due to impermanence; furthermore, there is a distinction between the permanent and the impermanent.
Now, regarding the clarified meaning of the Mahāyāna: though non-dual, it appears as dual; through provisional names and designations, it is opened into the shallow and the deep.

Thus, the distinctions between the superior and the inferior clearly manifest in many forms. There are three meanings of "cause": first, the fulfillment of causes; second, the movement toward the absence of ignorance.
The explanation of the three fruits is obscure because they possess three meanings. The fruits themselves also have three meanings: first, the fulfillment of the fruit;
second, the essence of non-delusion; and third, the ultimate fruit. Therefore, they are clear. How is this known?

A sutra states that a Bodhisattva in their final body sees only the end, not the beginning, whereas a Bodhisattva in a previous body has limited vision. Furthermore, the *Ratnavyuha Sutra* (Yingluo jing) says: "Vajra..."

Regarding the "Mind-Bodhisattva of a Hundred Kalpas": because they train in the majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*) of the Buddha, they are known as those who have attained clarity regarding the Buddha.
If there were not many supreme meanings, they would simply be equal to the Buddhas; however, they are still obscured by conditions. Question:

How can this Bodhisattva of the Golden Mind produce clear understanding? Answer: The Treatise says: It must be through the preceding Vajra-like mind that one realizes clear understanding, yet is unable to eliminate delusions (*moha*). This is due to being reflected upon...
Because it is moistened, the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) arises and comes to exist. Question:

Since this [state] arises from this very grade (*pakṣa*), at the time it first arises, why is it suddenly able to subdue and eliminate [the previous state]? Answer: There are indeed such cases. This is truly because of the accumulated power of the clarity of the preceding mind;
although it has already been produced by that [preceding state], it must still rely on the power of the prior understanding for its subsequent subtle refinement.

It increases and excels; therefore, it is further able to possess the power of removal. There is no difference in the case of that which arises from wood, yet it is further able to possess the function of burning the wood.
By this principle, one should understand that because something exists, it is further able to remove [that which opposes it]. This is the clarified meaning of the Mahāyāna:

prior to the "Golden Mind," there is a subtle state of *upalambha* (grasping at objects) from which the moisture that gives rise to the Golden Mind emerges. Within the Golden Mind, there remains the mind that grasps at objects.

"Exhaustion" (*kṣaya*) is a provisional designation because the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) is directed toward either existence or non-existence. When names are analyzed, there is nothing that is not thus;
these various meanings differ fundamentally from the explanations of the masters (*ācārya*).

Although it is now said that [existence] may exist or not exist, and that existence is removed or not removed, both removal and non-removal are merely skillful means (*upāya*). Furthermore, the masters explain the severance of the adamantine mind.
Regarding whether [the ignorance] is exhausted or not exhausted, the various Dharma masters of past and present have transmitted differing views.

Masters such as Zhuangyan and others have recounted that the diamond-like mind (*vajra-citta*) severs it, or that it is exhausted; however, they merely transmit the meaning of impermanence, which differs from the Buddha’s teaching.

According to their doctrinal school, if it were the fundamental ignorance (*avidyā*) beyond the two truths, it would be either something obtained through causes or something severed by the diamond-like mind. Why is this? Or...
The fact that causes are empty is the True Truth (*satyadharma*). The *Vajracittatattvasrota* chapter is sometimes called "Severance" or "Cessation.

Because the Buddha is the ultimate existence, and true existence transcends the two truths of arising and cessation, he does not undergo severance. Thus, it is said in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-alaṃkāra-karmavibhāga-sūtra*:

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (Exposition of Meaning) states: "When the Bodhisattva Vajracitta ascends the summit of a great mountain and enters hundreds of thousands of samādhis, he gathers the majestic deportment of the Buddhas to occupy that seat.
His knowledge and vision—whether regarding the permanent or the impermanent, and all objects and wisdoms—should be understood as being like those of a Buddha;

this is what is meant by 'training as a Buddha. Furthermore, when the sūtras speak of the 'wisdom and abandonment of a Buddha's bodhi,' they mean awakening to the bodhi and abandoning [the defilements] of a Buddha."
Question: If the Bodhisattva Vajra has severed or exhausted [afflictions], and is no different from a Buddha, why does a sutra say, "One who is like a Buddha is called an Awakened Buddha (Buddha)"?
In that case, one should simply say he is a Buddha. Furthermore, does the Vajra-mind arise through reflection and moistening (*pratibimba-ārdra*)?

Answer: If it were severed or exhausted, there would be no reflection or moistening. If it arises through reflection and moistening, then it must be that [the afflictions] have not been severed or fully exhausted.
The *Mahāyāna-zong-ru-furen-jing* states: "Because it is that which is severed by the Buddha’s bodhi-wisdom, the 'Golden Mind' has already severed or exhausted [the afflictions];
thus, the Buddha has nothing further to sever. However, the *Shizhu-duanjie-jing* states:

"The wisdom of a Bodhisattva at the stage of the Diamond Mind is such that all afflictions are like smoke—a subtle obstruction within meditative concentration. This refers to what is severed or [how it is severed]. As for...
"Obscured by subtle smoke" does not mean that there is still something like subtle smoke remaining. Second, masters such as Kaishan and others have transmitted the following account:

the gold-like mind is severed, yet it may not be entirely exhausted; only through the *bodhi* of a Buddha is it finally exhausted. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on Distinctions," states:
The Bodhisattva proceeds within the path of non-obstruction and proceeds within the liberation of all Buddhas.
Liberation from doubt is itself the severance of doubt; therefore, the *Sūtra on Severing the Fetters* states: "All Buddhas proceed within the path of liberation; this is the severance of doubt.

This is also as taught in the *Bhāryāsūtra* and other texts. Furthermore, it is clarified through reasoning: since the resolution of ignorance and the dispelling of delusion are correlative, it is logically necessary that this be so. Moreover...
An objection is raised: "If the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) has exhausted all delusions (*kleśa*), it should already be the Buddha.

Why, then, is it still a cause? Furthermore, why is this so? It is because there are still afflictions (*saṃkleśa*). According to the *Zhuangyan* school, the diamond-like mind’s liberation is not yet sufficient;

since its substance (*svabhāva*) still remains, it should therefore be the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), and thus the Buddha would be subject to suffering, impermanence, and so forth. The *Kaishan* school answers: "Alternatively, the delusions..."

Because the Buddhas of Response (Nirmāṇakāya) have merely suppressed [the afflictions] such as suffering, they no longer possess the capacity [to produce them]; thus, the great illumination reaches the point where the fruits of suffering and so forth do not arise.

This is precisely the meaning of the non-fulfillment of cause and effect. Therefore, according to that school's doctrine, this occurs from the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) within the seventh bhūmi and above.

If there is delusion as the cause but no fruit, it does not accord with the principle of cause and effect. Furthermore, according to the explicit meaning of the Mahāyāna, in every thought-moment, although the fruits of delusion have been accomplished, because the conditions for the causes differ, even when there is no delusion, one still encounters the principle that cause and effect do not correspond. Question:

If the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) either cuts off [delusions] or fails to exhaust them completely, how can it be called "diamond-like"? Answer: There are differing interpretations. Master Xian (Sengxian) said: "Although it is diamond..."
Because the adamantine [nature] is not yet exhausted, yet the multitudes are not burdened by it, it is called the "Weighing Adamant. Furthermore, it says:
"The adamantine mind’s subduing and severing is not the power of a single thought; it is like the provisional use of a sword to cut through a continuity.

The *Longguang* (Dragon Light) tradition follows the interpretation of Kaishan, holding that a single thought is itself provisional, and thus it is capable of subduing and severing. According to the interpretation of Master Xian, the provisional does not exist prior to or subsequent to [the moment].
The interpretations of Master Chuo differ in their respective positions regarding what follows. Regarding the question of why the *vajra* (diamond/thunderbolt) is indestructible:

if this mind cannot reach [the object], one might say it is due to being obscured by darkness; yet, since even the most subtle is investigated, is it not rather that the subtle itself causes it to be so?
If the body causes it to be obscured, then there is damage and affliction, and in that sense, it would not be a *vajra*. Answer: This is the explanation of the *vajra*-mind.
The internal state is clarity, not darkness; however, this is but a minor clarity that does not equal the true clarity of the Buddha. Therefore, it is called "darkness" only in relative terms.
This is not the same as the perceptions of ordinary beings, which may enter into the substance of the body. Question: Is the understanding of the substance itself the understanding of non-duality?
It should be designated according to such categories as patience (*kṣānti*) and joy (*prāmodya*), for the vajra-essence is free from doubt. Answer:
This principle applies generally across the vehicles. However, when distinguished according to the stages (*bhūmi*), its essence cannot be destroyed, yet it can exhaust all doubts;

thus, having reached this single stage of fulfillment, it alone receives the name "Vajra" within the Golden Mind (*suvarṇacitta*). This Mahāyāna meaning is discussed here according to a horizontal classification.

To fully understand [the distinction between] "having" and "not having," one must simply grasp the principle of "sameness. This is because, as the meaning of the bird's tracks in the sky illustrates, water differs from them yet possesses a sense of sameness.
This is the principle clarified in the Mahāyāna. Regarding the interpretation that these aspects may be mutually contradictory, this is elucidated through the provisional (upāya).

Therefore, the tenet of our school states: "The Vajra-mind is the primary discourse on mutual contradiction; the Buddha, however, is transcendent and without fruit. Thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Chapter... [text continues].
Five fascicles. At the very end of the "Chapter on Setting Forth" (*Prasthāna-parivarta*), it says:

"When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the six *pāramitās*, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), up to the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of a Buddha, and fully perfects all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*), thereby severing both afflictions (*kleśa*) and their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) while abiding in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), one should know that he is like a Buddha.
Yet, there are four points in which the two Buddhas differ: first, the perfection of causes versus the perfection of results..."

There are differences in fulfillment; second, differences in small views and extensive views; third, differences in permanence and non-permanence; fourth, differences in whether understanding is simultaneous or not.
Because there are these four meanings, there are also differences in clarity and obscurity, as previously explained. Yet the Sūtra speaks of "Equal Enlightenment" (Samyaksambodhi);

it is "equal" because the seeing is equal and the fulfillment is equal, yet in reality, they are not equal. Question: This is spoken from the perspective of the supreme. The Buddha is the adamantine essence (*vajra-kāya*).
This is because it is strange that all phenomena have been exhausted and nothing remains. The answer is that this meaning is indeed so.

Thus, the third fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, in the "Vajra-body Chapter," clarifies that the Buddha is vajra. However, if one examines the intent of this chapter, it takes only the sense of being eternal and indestructible as "vajra";
it does not discuss the cessation of effort to manifest that fulfillment is useless. Question: [What of] the ultimate study?
"This is the vajra. Since it possesses impermanence, how can it be compared to a vajra? Answer: It is explained through both non-differentiation and differentiation.
In reality, it is the final mind that is the true vajra; however, according to its manifest clarity, there is nothing that is not the vajra.
Furthermore, one may speak of it as possessing [the vajra-nature] within its own substance. Question: Is "vajra" a change of name? Answer: There must be four names.
First is the Vajra-mind, as previously described; second, the Vajra-samādhi; third, the Vajra-body; and fourth, the Vajra-wisdom.

These likewise correspond to their respective natures: the [first] two are categorized as having a body, which may be said to have the mind as the distant cause and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as the proximate condition;
the latter two are the essence and function. "Body" is a name for the essence, while "wisdom" is a name belonging to the function. Question:
How many names does this Great Sūtra have? Answer: It has five names. First is Śūraṅgama.
This means "formerly subdued," also "ultimate," also "vigorous concentration," and it is also called "cultivation. Second is Vajra, which is likened to being firm and sharp. Third is Prajñā;
it may be termed by way of its essential nature, or it may refer to wisdom. Fourth is Siṃhanāda, which is a simile.

In the *Abhayatā-nirdeśa*, the five [factors] are called "Buddha-nature" (*buddhadhātu*). They may be described as the essential nature (*svabhāva*), and they may also be described in terms of cause and effect.
The intention of that sutra is that, according to its various functions, it possesses immeasurable names. Question: That *vajra* is translated here as "diamond.
What is this "vajra-samādhi"? Answer: It is said to be made of superior gold; it is also said to be sharp iron. Question: Regarding this *vajra*...

Regarding the "Gold of the Mind" (*citta-suvarṇa*), the "Gold that is firm as diamond" (*vajra-dṛḍha-suvarṇa*) from the *Vajra-kāya-parivarta*, and the "Gold of the Golden Light" (*suvarṇaprabhāsa-suvarṇa*):

if one asks whether these are the same or different, the answer is that they are neither the same nor different. To speak briefly, while they may be described as the "Gold of the Golden Light," both the "Gold of the Golden Light" and the "Gold of the Vajra-kāya-parivarta" are explained in terms of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) at the stage of fruition. Therefore, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* answers: "The Vajra-body."

Regarding cause and effect: it clarifies that the *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding and indestructible, like a *vajra*. It clarifies that by taking the protection of the Dharma as the cause, one can attain this fruit of the *dharmakāya*;
thus, it establishes the cause by means of the fruit. The "Gold" in *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (*Golden Light*) is a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*.

The clarification regarding repentance, the offering of food, and so forth, indicates only differences in their general and specific attainments. There are two senses to the "Gold" of "solid gold": [the first is the *dharmakāya*, and the second refers to the physical substance].
Regarding the meaning: one aspect clarifies it through the True Dharma (saddharma), and one aspect clarifies it in terms of the causal stage. As for the fruit, it is *sarvajñā* (omniscience).

Therefore, the "gold" of the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) is discussed in relation to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samayaksaṃbodhi*). Although the "gold" of firmness is said to clarify *sarvajñā*, it is [so called] because it is luminous.

This refers to the cause; within the discussion of the cause, the lower stages are cited. If one speaks of *mahāprajñā*, it likewise does not refer solely to the intent of *nirvāṇa*, as it also extends to the stage of the fruit.
This concludes the meaning of the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) of the tenth stage.
*Wushi wude dasheng silun ji*, Scroll Two; *Dasheng silun xuanyi ji*, Scroll Five.
Regarding the Meaning of the Two Truths, there are ten sections:
First, elucidating the general purport; Second, elucidating the explanation of the names; Third, discussing the establishment [of the doctrine].

First, the explanation of names; second, the explanation of the provisional and the real; third, the explanation of the three natures; fourth, the clarification of existence and non-existence; fifth, the discernment of contemplative practice; sixth, the discussion of mutual identity;

seventh, the clarification of essence and characteristics; eighth, the discernment of the transcendence of names; ninth, the clarification of the inclusion of all phenomena; tenth, the clarification of sameness and difference.
First, the clarification of the general meaning. Regarding the Two Truths: in reality, they are neither prior nor posterior, nor are they simultaneous;

how could there be any numerical succession? It is merely for the sake of refuting the "Ten Layers" (shí chóng) of Kaishan Temple that they are explained as having no difference yet being differentiated.

To explain these ten layers and clarify the general meaning of the Two Truths, setting aside the differing terminology of various masters, there are briefly five schools. The first is the "Attainment of the *Satyasiddhi* (有所得成實)."
Regarding the masters of the Hinayana school: First, Dharma Master Yun of Guangzhai Temple said:
"The Two Truths are the profound essence of the sacred teachings and the deep repository of numinous wisdom. Second, Dharma Master Min of Zhuangyan Temple said:
"The Two Truths are indeed the supreme realm for dispelling delusions and the essential ford for entering the Path. Third, [Dharma Master] Zang of Kaishan Temple...

The Dharma Master [Seng]yun said: "The Two Truths are, in essence, the ultimate destination of the nature of dharmas (dharmatā); they are the supreme principle of the non-duality of the single reality.
The fourth school, Master Daoliang of Guo-bei Duobao Monastery in Guangzhou, said: "The Two Truths are, in essence, the general terminology of verbal teaching;
they are provisional designations based on mutual dependence, not the actual cause that exhaustively reaches the fundamental tenet. The fifth... [text fragment ends].
Regarding the *Wusuode Sanlun Dayi* (The Great Meaning of the Three Treatises on Non-Attainment) at Xiasi Temple on Mount She, Master Shuan states:
"The Two Truths are, in essence, the ultimate teaching for expressing principle and the wondrous instruction of words. Their substance is neither existence nor non-existence;

existence and non-existence do not permanently abide within that substance. Principle is neither one nor two; one and two do not contradict that principle. Now, following the Master’s explanation: [text continues].
Regarding the so-called two truths of the ultimate and the conventional: these are precisely existence and non-existence. Existence and non-existence together manifest a single path.

The Buddha, in accordance with conditions, taught the two doctrines of existence and non-existence, which run through all the scriptures. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains the tenfold two truths and the ten kinds of four truths, among others.
The ten-fascicle *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-mūla-karma Sūtra* states: "Because conventional truth exists, it is not empty; ultimate truth is empty."
Therefore, it is not existent. Because existence exists for ordinary beings, it is not empty; because non-existence is emptiness for the sages, it is not existent.
Existence is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and non-existence is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Thus, by following these two conditions, one speaks of the two truths.
In the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, Mañjuśrī asks: "Within the conventional truth, is there the ultimate truth? The first...
"Is there a conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) within the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*)? If it exists, then there would be only one truth;
if it does not exist, would this not mean that the Tathāgata has spoken falsely? The Buddha replied: "The conventional truth is itself the ultimate truth.

It is only through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, that I speak of two truths. The reason for clarifying these two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—is that I desire..."

Because there is that which is manifested, there is manifestation; yet manifestation does not exist [independently]. Because there is no manifestation, there is no non-existence. Thus, being neither existent nor non-existent, this is the Way that is manifested.
Existence and non-existence are the two truths; these are the teachings that manifest. The teaching is able to manifest the principle, and the principle is able to correspond to the teaching.

Because it accords with the principles of the teachings, it is called "Thus" (Tathāgata). Thus the Sūtra says: "Regarding all phenomena that exist or do not exist, one thoroughly realizes they are neither existent nor non-existent;
one does not cling to the dharma of non-duality, because there is neither 'one' nor 'two. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"The path of the Buddhas, the Holy Sovereigns, is subtle and extremely difficult to understand; it is not a realm of discursive thought, but is the sphere of activity only for the wise. This clarifies that there is nothing [to be grasped].
Attaining the two truths is not the realm of the *śrāvakas* or ordinary beings; rather, it is the sphere of activity for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Although it is not the realm of ordinary beings or the *śrāvakas*, it can nevertheless be attained as the realm of both the holy and the ordinary.

Although it is said to be the sphere of activity for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is not a sphere of activity for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas that involves anything to be attained (*upalabdha*). Therefore, the Great Sūtra says: "That which has attainment is called..."
It is ignorance. That which has nothing to be attained is called wisdom. Furthermore, that which has something to be attained belongs to the Two Vehicles;
that which has nothing to be attained is the Mahāyāna. That which has something to be attained is called the twenty-five states of existence;
that which has nothing to be attained is Great Nirvāṇa. That which has something to be attained has neither Path nor Fruit; that which has nothing to be attained possesses both Path and Fruit.

This is the result. The "Chapter on the Threefold Wisdom" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Whatever exists as a duality is called 'having attainment'; that which is without duality is called 'non-attainment.
What constitutes duality? It refers to the eye and form as a duality. If one says that the eye is the seer, it becomes distinct from form;
if form is the seen, it must necessarily differ from the eye and so forth. This is precisely what is called 'existence'."
This is what has been attained. According to the tenets of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* school, existence is indeed existent and non-existence is indeed nonexistent.

Therefore, they take the three types of existence as the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the nonexistence of things as the ultimate (*paramārtha*). Since this existence and nonexistence both abide within the realm of existence and nonexistence, there is nothing to be indicated.
Since there is nothing to be indicated, there is no principle that should be taught. When the teaching lacks this indication of the principle, the teaching itself lacks the capacity to express.
Principle cannot express itself; thus, principle is not the teaching of principle. Principle should not be the teaching; thus, it is not the teaching-principle.

Because it is not the teaching-principle, there is no principle. Because it is not the teaching of principle, it is not the teaching. Therefore, according to worldly dharmas, there are words but no meaning.
Now, however, these two teachings—existence and non-existence—manifest the Way that is neither existent nor non-existent. This [Way] is neither existent nor non-existent...

Therefore, there are two teachings: that of existence and that of non-existence. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Regarding the dharmas that emerge from the intermediate state, there are both words and meanings.

The meaning of the Mountain Gate (Shanmen) school often differs from that of the masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and other treatises. The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and others maintain that object (*ālambana*) and wisdom (*jñāna*) are two distinct things, each unrelated to the other;
that the object itself is designated as empty; that there are two types of wisdom regarding the two truths; and that wisdom arises of its own accord.

It ceases of itself. Objects have neither arising nor ceasing; this is a general judgment for the time being. However, if one discusses the matter in detail, both objects and cognition possess both arising and ceasing, as well as non-arising and non-ceasing.
Why is this? It is clarified that while the object of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) has neither arising nor ceasing, the object of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) does arise and cease.

Furthermore, while cognition within the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*) possesses arising and ceasing, cognition at the level of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) is without arising or ceasing. Such is the meaning.
It is not merely that there is something to be attained; it is also that one cannot [grasp] the meaning of the object of focus. Therefore, Vimalakīrti rebuked him, saying:

"Do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to speak of the Dharma of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Now, how could one possibly use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to take the realm of the true mark as its object?
I now maintain that the realm and wisdom are non-dual and mutually dependent; thus, while there are the realm and wisdom, they are identical to empty space.
Space is without arising and without cessation; wisdom is likewise without arising and without cessation. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The sublime realm of all Buddhas is like space.
This clarifies that the objective realm is identical to space. The "Chapter on the Threefold Wisdom" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:
"Because space arises, Prajñā arises," and so forth. The "Chapter on Emptiness" states, "Prajñā is empty," etc., clarifying that this wisdom is identical to space.
It is not merely that it is without arising and ceasing—thus being identical to space—but its arising and ceasing are likewise identical to space.
Just as space is without arising or ceasing yet possesses the functional capacity for arising and ceasing, so too do the object and wisdom lack arising and ceasing, yet possess arising and ceasing.

This is because it shares the same nature as empty space. Since the existence of empty space constitutes the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), and its non-existence is identical to empty space, the non-existence of empty space constitutes the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Furthermore, because existence is identical to empty space, the existence of empty space is provisional;
because non-existence is identical to empty space, the non-existence of empty space is real. Thus, both existence and non-existence pervade both the objective realm and cognitive wisdom.
Arising and ceasing also apply to both object and wisdom; however, this arising and ceasing is likewise identical to empty space.
Therefore, the arising and ceasing of empty space is taken as the arising and ceasing of object and wisdom. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "As empty space arises, so does prajñā arise.
This intention seeks to clarify that empty space takes non-arising as its arising, and prajñā likewise takes non-arising as its arising. Hence, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* says: [as cited in the source].

It says: "The practice of the stages is like empty space. That passage first explains that the object [of cognition] is identical to empty space—neither arising nor ceasing, transcending the three realms—and subsequently cites the practice of the stages to clarify that the practice of the stages is likewise neither arising nor ceasing, transcending the three realms.

The intention of the Mountain Gate (Shanmen) is that both the object and the wisdom are neither arising nor ceasing; this is eternally distinct from the Sāṃkhya school and others. As in the Sāṃkhya...
The treatises and other works state: "If there were existence for the manifest (*vijñapti*) and non-existence for the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), these would each possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because they possess characteristics, they would be objects of apprehension (*upalabdha*). To have an object of apprehension is to be outside of principle (*tattva*).

If, however, the manifest is not existent and the unmanifest is not non-existent—being neither existent nor non-existent—it is called 'characterless' (*alakṣaṇa*). Since the manifest is not existent, it lacks the characteristic of existence; since the unmanifest is not [non-existent]..."

Because there is no [existence], there is no characteristic of non-existence. Since there is neither the characteristic of existence nor the characteristic of non-existence, it is called "non-apprehension.

That which is non-apprehensible is precisely what is termed "within the principle" (*li-nei*). Regarding the definitive (*nītārtha*) and the non-definitive (*neyārtha*): if there is manifestation, it is not existent; if there is non-manifestation, it is not non-existent.
That which posits that the manifest exists and the unmanifest does not exist is called "provisional meaning" (neyārtha).

That which posits that existence exists and non-existence does not exist is called the "esoteric treasury" (guhyakośa). That which posits that the manifest does not exist and the unmanifest is not non-existent—[this is the definitive meaning].
This is called "revealing the secret. To reveal the secret is called "definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*). That which is a secret treasury is called "non-definitive meaning" (*neyārtha*).
Non-definitive meaning is called the "half-syllable," while definitive meaning is called the "full-syllable. The full-syllable is named the Mahāyāna; the half-syllable is named the Hīnayāna.
Because the Hīnayāna is non-definitive, it is said to involve "attainment of something"; because it is definitive...
It is called "non-attainment. Therefore, there are no two truths. Ordinary beings, sages, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas all practice together; yet there is attainment and there is loss.
If one holds that existence is truly existent and non-existence is truly nonexistent, this is called "loss.

If one holds that existence is not [ultimately] existent and non-existence is not [ultimately] nonexistent, this is called "attainment. Because one realizes that existence is not [ultimately] existent, one is therefore called a "sage. [Regarding] existence...
Because these exist, they are called "ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*). Thus it is said that there has never been duality;

it is only by way of the two aspects of gain and loss that the distinction between ordinary persons and sages (*ārya*) is established, even extending to the difference between birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The Vaipulya [teachings] are also called 'ambrosia' (*amṛta*) and also called 'poison. If taken and digested, they are medicine; if not digested, they are poison. When a single medicine...
It was once sweet poison; however, it is only because of the two conditions of having or lacking skillful means that the distinction between poisonous medicine and nectar arises.
Question: The Sāṃkhya teachers and others also say that the objects of the two truths are traversed by both ordinary beings and sages.

Now you also say they are traversed by both ordinary beings and sages; how does this differ from their claim? Answer: They say that the eight worldly dharmas are not the objects of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

They differ. It is simply that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are attached because they grasp at signs (*nimitta*), whereas noble ones (*ārya*) emerge from true contemplation and act with the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) of the Path, and thus are not attached;

this is the difference. Now it is clarified that ordinary beings say that existence can be existent and non-existence can be nonexistent, whereas noble ones know that existence is not existent and know that non-existence is not nonexistent;
therefore, they differ from those [ordinary beings]. Question: If noble ones manifest neither existence nor non-existence, how is it so?
It is not that they do not exist. As for the claim that the "existence" and "non-existence" of ordinary beings merely refer to existence and non-existence:

since the principles and teachings regarding ordinary beings and sages differ fundamentally and eternally, how can one say that the two truths are practiced in common by both ordinary beings and sages? Answer: Although the names of the two truths are the same, their underlying meanings are vastly different.

In ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), existence indicates existence; non-existence indicates non-existence. In noble ones (*ārya*), existence indicates non-existence; non-existence indicates non-non-existence.
Thus, although the names used are the same, they differ according to the presence or absence [of realization] in these two types of persons—the ordinary and the noble.

Since for the ordinary person existence indicates existence, existence cannot be transformed into non-existence. Now, since it cannot be transformed into non-existence, the ordinary person is likewise not [an ārya].
One can be transformed into a sage. For a sage, "existence" (yu) already signifies "non-existence" (bu you), and "non-existence" (wu) already signifies "not non-existence" (bu wu).

Therefore, what is attained as existence can be transformed into non-existence. An ordinary person can be transformed into a sage. Since an ordinary person possesses existence, their afflictions (*kleśa*) are indeed afflictions;
they cannot be rendered non-afflictive. Now, when a sage speaks of existence, it signifies non-existence. That is to say...

Afflictions are transformed into non-affliction; therefore, although afflictions exist, they are as if non-existent. Yet the nature of afflictions is fundamentally non-existent, for it has no being whatsoever.
It is conventionally designated as "ignorance" (avidyā), such that what exists is transformed into non-existence.

Question: When one speaks of existence and non-existence, it is to indicate that which is neither existent nor non-existent, so that sentient beings may, by means of the teaching of existence and non-existence, realize [the truth].
Regarding the True Path that is neither existent nor non-existent: for what reason do you not directly teach the Middle Way of neither existence nor non-existence so that beings may attain awakening?

Instead, why do you speak of existence and non-existence, causing people to fall into the affliction of existence and non-existence? It seems as though you intentionally wish to cause sentient beings to dwell outside the principle, in the human realm and the hells, due to the causes and conditions of their afflictions.
[Question: Sentient beings are inverted; perhaps it is because of their minds... [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

They cannot be awakened to suddenly; they must be transformed through the gradual teaching. However, if sentient beings hear of "existence" they cling to existence, and if they hear of "non-existence" they become obstructed by non-existence.
Thus, when one speaks of that which is neither existent nor non-existent, they fail to receive the transformation. Therefore, the Buddha and sentient beings share the same source.
It is not because of the *saṃnāha* (great armor/vow) that the Noble Ones employ the skillful means of compassion to transform beings.

For example, it is like an elder who removes his precious, fine robes and puts on soiled, greasy clothes to work together with his sons in the manure pit; this is precisely acting in accordance with conditions.

Even though the Noble Ones employ skillful means to temporarily conform to sentient beings, therefore, when the world speaks of a self, they also speak of there being one; when the world speaks of no-self, they also speak of there being none.

Subsequently, when one seeks its existence or non-existence, neither can be apprehended. To cause one to realize that existence and non-existence are neither existent nor non-existent—this is the state where existence and non-existence are neither existent nor non-existent; it is the non-existence of both existence and non-existence. Question:

If existence and non-existence are used to represent that which is neither existent nor non-existent, so as to lead to the realization of the Middle Way of neither existence nor non-existence, then would the two teachings of existence and non-existence be discarded?
Does it not depart? If one realizes the principle, the teaching is abandoned; because the teaching is abandoned, the principle should also be abandoned.

However, when one realizes that which is neither existent nor non-existent, the teachings of existence and non-existence are not abandoned. Therefore, from the principle of being neither existent nor non-existent, the non-dual teaching arises.

What is the difference between "breaking through the conventional to enter the ultimate" and "emerging from the ultimate to manifest the conventional," as well as the *Dilun* school’s "stopping delusion to return to the ultimate" and "arising from the ultimate to function"?

Answer: Those masters maintain that there are two distinct realms—the conventional and the ultimate—therefore they speak of breaking through the conventional to enter the ultimate, and subsequently emerging from the ultimate to manifest the conventional;

their method of stopping delusion is likewise based on this duality. Now, by clarifying "existence and non-existence," we refute the attachment to existence. This is explained as follows: [The text continues with the clarification of non-existence.]

There is neither non-existence nor existence. This is to destroy the malady of nihilism. Once the two maladies of existence and non-existence are eliminated, what further dualistic teaching could there be to obtain?
Since no dualistic teaching can be obtained, what principle of "neither existence nor non-existence" could there be to realize?

Therefore, it is neither existent nor non-existent, and it is also not "neither existent nor non-existent. Thus, existence, non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence all vanish into stillness.
It is boundless. Thus, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* states: "One does not depart from words and letters to explain the meaning of liberation. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"These words neither abide nor do they not abide, because these words have no inherent existence. Question:

If this is so, you have merely seen the refutation of outsiders' teachings on existence and non-existence by stating that it is "neither existent nor non-existent. How can you claim that this represents the Buddha’s teaching on the two truths?

Is it the Way that is neither existent nor non-existent? The answer is: It is precisely the teaching that causes one to realize that existence is not existence, and non-existence is not non-existence;
this is both a refutation and a teaching. Furthermore, if all dharmas were originally existent, they could be manifested as non-existent, involving either gain or loss.
However, since they are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning, they are only provisionally designated as existent through conventional names. There is only the fundamental [reality].

It does not exist. Because it does not exist, it is provisionally designated as "existing. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "Subhūti does not destroy conventional designations when he speaks of the meaning of the true mark (*dharmatā*);
nor does he move from the true mark when he speaks of conventional designations. Therefore, his mind does not waver regarding existence or non-existence. Question:
Originally, one relies upon the two teachings of existence and non-existence to realize the Way that is neither existent nor non-existent. Now, if there is neither existence nor non-existence...
If it is not that both [existence and non-existence] are exhausted together, how could this not be falling into a false view? Answer:

Originally, it was because one might think that existence can become non-existence, or that non-existence can become existence, that it was clarified that the manifestation of existence is not existence, and the manifestation of non-existence is not non-existence. Thus, the teaching of existence and non-existence was used to manifest the Way that is neither existent nor non-existent.

Now, if the two maladies of existence and non-existence no longer exist, what further use would there be for these two teachings? Since the teachings are no longer discussed, [the question does not arise].

Furthermore, what principle of "neither being nor non-being" could possibly be found? Thus, the principles and teachings regarding existence and non-existence, as well as neither being nor non-being, are by nature pure.
It is only because of deluded sentient beings that these become objects of fear. As the *Śata-śāstra* says: "What defilement can there be in an object of fear? Question:
If both principle and teaching are entirely pure, why is it necessary to teach the doctrine of the two truths? Answer: [The details are] as follows:

As previously stated, it must be taught for the sake of curing the illnesses of sentient beings. However, one speaks of existence precisely because one does not abide in existence, and speaks of emptiness because one does not abide in emptiness.

One speaks of existence while not abiding in existence; one speaks of emptiness while not abiding in emptiness. To designate emptiness as existence and to designate existence as emptiness—this existence is non-existence, and this existence is an emptiness that is not empty.
Existence and emptiness constitute the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); the existence within emptiness constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The fundamental principle is established by abiding in the *prajñāpāramitā* through the dharma of non-abiding.
The end of the fifth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Good son, the Tathāgata sometimes explains one as three, and explains three as one."

Furthermore, the *Brahmacarya-parivarta* states: "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, possesses great skillful means (*upāya*). He speaks of the impermanent as permanent, and the permanent as impermanent;
he speaks of pleasure as suffering, and suffering as pleasure. All categories of phenomena, such as self and purity, are likewise so. Furthermore, the *Guṇarāja-parivarta* states:
"Because one has eternally severed the twenty-five realms of existence (*bhava*), it is named 'purity. Purity is precisely *nirvāṇa*; it is also like this."
Nirvāṇa is designated as "existent," yet this nirvāṇa is in reality not existent. The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, speak of nirvāṇa as being existent in accordance with worldly convention.
It is just as people in the world call one who is not their father "father" and one who is not their mother "mother"; nirvāṇa is likewise so.
It is spoken thus in accordance with worldly convention, saying that all Buddhas possess Great Nirvāṇa. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One is immeasurable;
immeasurable is one. Many are one; one is many," and so forth.

Second, the explanation of the names. Regarding what is called the "Two Truths": the *satya* of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-satya*) is also termed the "Truth of the Ultimate Meaning" (*paramārtha-satya*), and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is also termed the "Worldly Truth" (*loka-satya*).

To explain these names according to their characters: "ultimate" (*parama*) takes "reality" (*tattva*) as its meaning; because that which exists is not non-existent and its essence is devoid of falsehood, it is called the "Ultimate Truth.
As for "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*), there is nothing that surpasses it in its extreme profundity; thus it is called "ultimate. This refers to the intended purport.

Because it is real, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*). The conventional (*saṃvṛti*) takes falsehood as its meaning. Existing things are not substantial in nature; they are established in dependence upon various conditions.
