"I say that phenomena produced through causes and conditions are 'non-existent,' yet they are also provisional designations, and this is the meaning of the Middle Way. There are many such passages; I have cited them here briefly. This is intended to clarify all...
The Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent. The Sage speaks of existence and non-existence within the context of conventional designations.
Sentient beings do not understand this intent and give rise to much attachment. Hearing the word "existence," they take it to mean definitely existent; such existence is the view of eternalism.

Hearing the word "non-existence," they take it to mean definitely non-existent; such non-existence is the view of annihilationism. Even the sixty-two views arise from this, whereby one loses the Middle Way. Furthermore...
They are deluded regarding provisional function. A Great Sūtra states: "Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas perceive only emptiness and do not perceive non-emptiness;

they do not practice the Middle Way. Because they do not practice the Middle Way, they do not perceive the Buddha-nature. This passage serves as proof that they have lost the Middle Way. Furthermore, it says:
"At one time, while I was discussing conventional truth with Maitreya Bodhisattva, five hundred śrāvakas were completely unaware [of what was being said]."

Regarding the understanding of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): even those who practice the proximate stages of devotion do not yet understand it; how then could this consciousness fathom the profound and distant ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)?

Thus, one realizes that [this consciousness] is deluded regarding provisional names (*prajñapti*). If one is deluded within the midst of the conventional, there are five errors: first, the error of making all dharmas—which are non-dual—into two distinct meanings;

second, the error of making the provisional names of all dharmas into substantial natures (*svabhāva*); third, the error of making the mutual dependence of all dharmas into intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*); fourth...
To lose the fact that all phenomena are empty and instead establish them as having an intrinsic nature is the fifth loss: it turns the Middle Way into an extreme view.

If a person has long cultivated skillful means, they will understand the path that is neither existent nor non-existent—that which is the domain of the six consciousnesses. They know that existence is non-existence, and non-existence is not non-existence;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither dual nor non-dual. This is the ultimate Way. Thus, the Great Sūtra says: "The wise one sees..."

Emptiness and non-emptiness: by practicing the Middle Way, one perceives the Buddha-nature. Having understood the Middle and recognized the conventional nature of phenomena, there are five attainments that correspond to the aforementioned faults:
first, understanding that all dharmas are non-dual; second, knowing that all dharmas are merely provisional names; third, understanding that all dharmas exist in mutual dependence;
fourth, awakening to the fact that all dharmas are empty; and fifth, perceiving the Middle Way. This is the doctrine of the Mountain Gate (the Buddhist monastic community).
This is the practice of contemplation that is non-apprehension. "Small" refers to the Small Vehicle and "Great" refers to the Great Vehicle, as clarified in the *Śata-śāstra*.
This is the True Dharma because it is neither great nor small; thus, the designations "great" and "small" are established through mutual dependence to clarify their distinction.
If it were neither great nor small, yet were both great and small, this would be a vertical (hierarchical) discourse. If it is great because it depends on the small, [then...]
The great is small; this is a horizontal discussion. Thus, the "great" is called "small-great," and the "small" is called "great-small.

Furthermore, existence depends on non-existence, and because of non-existence there is existence. The name "existence" arises within the name "non-existence," and the name "non-existence" arises within the name "existence.

Therefore, existence and non-existence are termed "non-existence and existence. Taking the name "non-existence and existence" constitutes the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya); [taking] the name "existence and non-existence..."
These constitute the two truths. Regarding these two truths, which exist as provisional designations, sentient beings are inverted;

they perceive that which does not exist as existing, forming the notion that it exists. Because they follow after existence as being existent, they see form as form, and so on, up to seeing mind as mind.
Once they see form as having existence, the mind then becomes the mind of form. Thus, regarding all that is transmitted, if one is correctly attached during a state of inversion—
They cannot be transformed. However, when those attached to existence become weary of toil and suffering at a later time and desire liberation, the Buddha speaks thus:

"There is no beginning to that which fundamentally does not exist. This is one stage of transformation upon awakening to the non-existence of attainment and the detachment from mind, form, and existence.

Next, because following the non-existence of all phenomena leads to the formation of nihilistic views, the followers of the Two Vehicles cling to emptiness, while ordinary beings [cling to existence].

Stuck in existence, I shall now further explain emptiness and non-emptiness. Thereupon, one attains the realization that even a single form or a single fragrance has, from its very origin, been neither existent nor non-existent.

One awakens to the Middle Way and correct contemplation (*samyak-darśana*). Now, regarding this awakening through contemplation, it is appropriate to designate the name of the contemplation itself as the "Middle Way.
Next, that which is neither existent nor non-existent yet is provisionally named "non-existence" is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). This clarifies [the distinction].

That which is provisionally existent is not called "existent," and that which is provisionally existent is not called "non-existent. This clarifies that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is a provisional existence that is neither existent nor non-existent;

by fully severing the two views of eternalism and nihilism, it is termed the contemplation of conventional truth. Next, because it relies upon conventional truth, it is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*);

because it relies upon provisional existence, the name "ultimate truth" is itself a provisional non-existence. That which is a provisional non-existence is not called "non-existent," for it is a provisional non-existence.

It is neither called "non-existent" nor "not non-existent. Therefore, the contemplation of the provisional non-existence of ultimate truth also fully eliminates both views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Provisional names are ultimate truth; since ultimate truth is thus, it applies even to such categories as provisional names for *buddhatā* (Buddha-nature) and *nirvāṇa*.
Because it cuts back [extremes], it is called the Middle Way. Regarding phenomena, the Middle Way is immeasurable; yet, if even the Middle Way cannot be made into one, how could there possibly be...?
Many masters have now clarified the Middle Way by means of the Dharma. They clarify that all phenomena belong to the category of provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

Since this already clarifies the contemplation of the ultimate and the conventional, sentient beings should accordingly practice the contemplation of the Middle Way within the Two Truths. Now, it is clarified that even the conventional and the ultimate are neither truly existent nor non-existent;
even the ultimate and the conventional are neither conventional nor non-conventional. If even the ultimate and the conventional do not exist, how could there be a Middle Way of the Two Truths?
It can be attained; therefore, it is neither true nor conventional. Consequently, in reality, there is no meaning of the three contemplations.
Thus, the "Chapter on Equality" in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The mark of the equality of all dharmas is such that all noble ones cannot practice it and cannot reach it.

Furthermore, the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva’s Teaching and Transformation," states: "Before a World-Buddha appears in the world, there are no names, no names for meanings, and no essence."

In reality, there are no names for the three realms, nor for good and evil, the six destinies, and so forth; it is only because the Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of sentient beings that he spoke of the three realms, the six destinies, and the like.
If this is so, where does the principle of the two truths exist as something natural?
Sixth, the mutual identity of the two truths (*dvayasatya*). The mutual identity of the two truths is fully set forth in numerous sūtras.
For example, in the twelfth fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the Buddha answers Mañjuśrī, saying: "The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, in the "Offering of the Bowl" chapter, states: "Form (*rūpa*) is emptiness (*śūnyatā*); emptiness is form. The meaning of their mutual identity in other sūtras may be sought accordingly. Next, if one says...

To say that "the ultimate is the conventional" and "the conventional is the ultimate" is a grandiose argument (*śe-lun*). To say that "form is emptiness" and "emptiness is form" is a precise argument (*che-lun*).
Although they differ in being grandiose or precise, they both equally clarify the meaning of mutual identity (*xiang-ji*). However, this is the interpretation of the Chengshi masters.
There are two interpretations of "mutual identity" (*xiāngjí*). The first states that the two truths have distinct essences yet occupy the same locus; therefore, they are called mutually identical.

The second states that because they are of one essence, they are said to be mutually identical; this is the sense of "identity as such. Thus, Kaishan said: "The provisional lacks its own substance; it arises and yet is not existent.
The conventional is the ultimate, for being without substance it can be provisional; the ultimate is precisely the conventional. Now, I say:
This is not so. Since the two truths are said to be of one essence, how could there be entering or emerging from contemplation prior to the seventh stage?

And how could there be two truths that can be contemplated simultaneously from the eighth stage upward? Furthermore, if something arises due to causes and conditions, it is "identical" (interpenetrating);
if it does not require causes to arise, it is not identical. If it arises in accordance with false causes, then there is identity.

If something is established by a true cause, then it is not identical [to its opposite]. As the School of Ornamentation (Zhuāngyán jiā) says: "Nirvāṇa is a wondrous existence that transcends the two truths.
This wondrous existence is not identical to non-existence; because empty space is not obtained through karmic causes, and because it is eternally pervasive, it is not identical to existence.
The School of Opening the Good (Kāi shàn děng) says: "The fruit of Buddhahood is subsumed within the two truths," and so forth.
Since these two—reading and waiting—are established through conventional designation, one might say they are mutually identical. Now, I say this is not so.

How could the dharmas produced by two causes be non-identical with the causal essence from which they arise? Furthermore, if the conventional were identical with the ultimate, yet the conventional still persisted, [it would contradict the nature of the ultimate].

If the conventional were outside of the ultimate, how could it be identical to the ultimate? If it were identical to the ultimate and not different from it, how could one still insist on distinguishing that the conventional exists?
If one were to insist on distinguishing the ultimate as being the conventional, one would be distinguishing emptiness as form and form as emptiness.
If this were so, would it not contradict the sutras? Now, we speak of "existence" in accordance with provisional designations; this is non-existence.
Because it exists [as a conventional designation], it is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). A provisional name is called "non-existent";

this is a non-existence that is not non-existent, and thus it constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since existence is an existence that is not existent, it is not an existence apart from non-existence.
Since non-existence is a non-existence that is not non-existent, it is not a non-existence apart from existence. Since non-existence is not a non-existence apart from existence, therefore...
There is no "non-existence" external to existence. Since existence is not an existence distinct from non-existence, there is no "existence" external to non-existence.

Because there is no existence external to non-existence, existence would then be separate from non-existence; yet there is no non-existence external to existence, for non-existence would then be separate from existence.

Since non-existence is already separate from both existence and non-existence, non-existence is itself existence, and thus there is no non-existence. Since that which is separate from non-existence does not exist, existence is itself non-existence, and thus there is no existence. Therefore, [neither exists].

It is neither non-existent nor existent; it is neither the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) nor the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet it clarifies both the ultimate and the conventional. The conventional is the ultimate conventionality, and the ultimate is the conventional ultimacy.

Therefore, non-existence is identical to existence, for this is not an existence that exists despite being non-existent. Existence is identical to non-existence, for this is not a non-existence that is separate from existence.

Thus, because it is not an existence that exists despite being non-existent, it is called "existence-non-existence. Because it is not a non-existence that exists despite being non-existent, it is called "non-existence-existence. If there were no...
That which is "not existent" is the non-existence that is divorced from existence.

If there were an existence that was not non-existent, it would be an existence divorced from non-existence—such as the existence of the three provisional designations (*prajñapti*). That which is the non-existence of space and so forth is the non-existence that is distinct from existence.

Now, it is said that since existence is an existence that is not-existent, existence is itself non-existence; and since non-existence is a non-existence that is not-non-existent, non-existence is itself existence.

If there were an existence distinct from non-existence, or a non-existence distinct from existence, then one would use existence to differentiate non-existence, because that would be an existence distinct from non-existence;
or one would use non-existence to differentiate existence, because that would be a non-existence distinct from existence. [But such is not the case. Non-existence...
Since it is free from both existence and non-existence, the name "non-existent" arises only with respect to non-existence;

and since existence is an existence that is distinct from non-existence, the name "existent" arises only with respect to existence. Since these two names, "existence" and "non-existence," do not interpenetrate, how could the two essences—the ultimate and the conventional—be identical?
Therefore, regarding the names "ultimate" and "conventional," if they function as one, their identity is not discussed; if the names differ, their functions differ.

Nor do we discuss identity (*tādātmya*). Now, regarding the Mahāyāna meaning of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*): because they are one yet different, we discuss identity; because difference is one, we discuss distinction (*vyatireka*).
If there were oneness with difference, it would be like the two truths being one essence with two functions; in that case, we would not discuss distinction.
If there were difference with oneness, it would be like the two functions being one essence; in that case as well, we would not discuss identity. Why? Because of the essence (*svabhāva*).

In each case, there is no sense of identity; the principle of function differs, and thus there is likewise no sense of identity. Now, it is said that they are identical because while the name is one, the functions differ;
they are identical because while the function is one, the names differ. This is the mutual identity of name and function, and of unity and difference.
If existence were truly existent, it would not be identical to emptiness; if emptiness were truly empty, emptiness would not be identical to existence. This, then, is...

Regarding the statement that while emptiness (*śūnyatā*) differs from both name and function, it is now clarified that they are identical (*lakṣaṇa-ekībhāva*): one must first cleanse the former [distinctions] until they are entirely purified, and only then may this be explained.
If the meaning of the identity between form (*rūpa*) and emptiness is revealed, other dharmas may be inferred by analogy.

Why? Because it is said that "form is non-form. Form is the emptiness of non-form; emptiness is the non-emptiness of non-emptiness; and non-emptiness is the emptiness of non-emptiness. Therefore, it is emptiness.

Form can be identified with characteristics; because it both exists and does not exist, existence can be identified with emptiness. Emptiness is not a non-empty emptiness; emptiness can be identified with existence. Because it can be identified with existence, it is called "emptiness-as-existence.
Because existence can be identified with emptiness, it is called "existence-as-emptiness. Because there is existence-as-emptiness, it differs from mere existence and from non-existent emptiness.
Because there is emptiness-as-existence, it differs from mere emptiness and from non-existent existence. If existence were not emptiness-as-existence, [it would be mere existence].

If existence is not identical to emptiness, and emptiness does not exist within existence, and emptiness is neither identical to existence nor non-identical to existence, then one cannot establish the principle of mutual identity (*xiāngjí*).
Since existence is not identical to emptiness, there is likewise no mutual identity; therefore, as emptiness and existence are distinct, the meaning of mutual identity does not apply.
The masters of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and others say: "When causes and conditions are found to have no substantial essence, this is called the 'True' (*zhēn*). The True is the conventional (*sú*)."

"It is precisely the ultimate (paramārtha). Apart from the ultimate there is no conventional (saṃvṛti); apart from the conventional there is no ultimate. Now I say this is not so. If your ultimate is identical to the conventional, then you lose the ultimate;

if the conventional is identical to the ultimate, then you lose the conventional. If the ultimate and the conventional exclude one another like the tips of two opposing tusks, what conventional thing could possibly be identical [to the ultimate]?
Furthermore, if you hold that the signless (animitta) is the ultimate and the characterized (sanimitta) is the conventional, I now ask you: is "existence" (bhāva) not empty (śūnya)?

Existence exists; thus it is separate from emptiness. Emptiness is not existence. Emptiness is separate from existence; since emptiness is already separate from existence, existence lies outside of emptiness.
Since existence is already separate from emptiness, existence lies outside of emptiness. If existence lies outside of emptiness, how can they be identical?

If it did not lie outside, why would those at the seventh stage and below need to exert themselves in entering and emerging from contemplation? Since existence and non-existence are distinct, they cannot be identical.

It is precisely so. The meaning of "non-attainment" now is this: emptiness is not empty of itself; therefore, it is called "emptiness that possesses existence. Existence is not existent of itself; therefore, it is called "existence that is for the sake of emptiness.
Since it is an existence that is empty, it is devoid of an emptiness apart from existence. Since emptiness is the emptiness of existence, it is devoid of an existence apart from emptiness.
Because it is devoid of an existence apart from emptiness, existence is itself emptiness. Because it is devoid of an emptiness apart from existence, emptiness is itself [existence].
Because it exists, it is said that "form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. Apart from form there is no emptiness; apart from emptiness there is no form.

The old commentaries on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* state: "Form is emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness. The very nature of form is itself empty."
The nature of color is itself emptiness; it is not that emptiness is attained by destroying color. This clarifies that the intrinsic nature of this color is identical to emptiness.
For example, if color were "good" while "good" were not color, then "good" would belong to the category of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Now, we say this is not so: color is itself emptiness.

If color were a sensory object (*rūpāyatana*) and "good" were a mental object, then when color is burned, the mental object should not be burned. If both were to be burned, [then they would be the same].
Taking this as an illustration: if form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) were two distinct things, then one would be combustible while the other would not be combustible.
Furthermore, since both are equally form, [they cannot be separate]. Now, it is clarified that the text of this sūtra is precisely the correct meaning:

"Form is itself emptiness; it is not that emptiness arises from the extinction of form. This means that this form is the form of emptiness, and emptiness is the emptiness of form. Because form is empty, the very nature of form is itself empty.
Because emptiness is form, emptiness itself is form; this is called "emptiness as form. Emptiness and form are neither identical nor different, neither existent nor non-existent.
They are provisionally distinguished as "emptiness" and "form," and thus emptiness is designated as form and form is designated as emptiness.

Therefore, form is itself emptiness and emptiness is itself form. It is not that form ceases to exist for it to become emptiness; rather, the very nature of form is itself empty. [Question: Regarding the conventional...

Regarding "that which is identical to reality": when a wheel is turning, does reality also turn? The ancient response was: "When it is a conventional wheel, reality should not turn; it does not turn. Question:
If that were so, the identity of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) would not be clarified. Since you speak of their mutual identity, then reality ought to be turned.
If one turns while the other does not, then they are not identical. Furthermore, as for form (*rūpa*) and so forth, which exist originally and now...
There is no time [when it does not exist]; even true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) has only begun to exist. If true emptiness were originally existent, what would this emptiness be empty of?

Furthermore, they are not identical. If one says that true emptiness is neither original nor beginning, then it is also neither identical nor non-identical, neither principle nor non-principle, neither truth nor non-truth, and so forth.
To say that various truths and such are "originally and beginningly identical" is merely a provisional expression; the preceding refers to the original...

Emptiness and form exist sequentially, as one precedes the other; therefore, they do not coincide. Now it is said that emptiness and form—true emptiness and [conventional] form—do not obstruct one another; hence, there is no hindrance.

Seventh, the clarification of the essence and characteristics. Regarding the essence of the two truths, the masters' explanations differ, as is fully explained in the section on the fivefold Middle Way.
Now, this shall be further elucidated. One school asserts that the two truths take existence (*bhāva*) as their essence, while emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is their meaning.
The reason for this is that emptiness exists because of existence; is it not the case, then, that one discusses emptiness on the basis of existence?

Emptiness takes existence as its substance, while existence takes emptiness as its functional meaning. Thus, the *Kulaputra-sūtra* states: "To penetrate the five aggregates of clinging as empty is the meaning of suffering. Now, I say this is not so.
If one says that existence is the substance, then existence should be the principle. If not...
If this principle is empty, then it is not a principle; yet there must also be such a truth, for there is no "non-existence" that is not itself a truth.

Second, [the opponent claims] that the two truths take emptiness as their essence and existence as their functional utility; thus, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and others, emptiness is the foundation of all phenomena.
This too is not so, and it shall be refuted by analogy. Since existence and non-existence are distinct, and permanence and impermanence are distinct, how could...?

To "attain" is to take [existence] as the essence. Third, if the two truths each have their own distinct essence—where existence takes existence as its essence and emptiness takes emptiness as its essence—this is not the case here.
If each truth possessed its own separate essence, they would constitute two distinct principles that could not be identical with one another.
Yet, the sutra states: "Form is itself emptiness; emptiness is itself form. How, then, could there be two separate essences? Fourth, the two...
The two truths share a single essence; they are distinguished according to two perspectives. If one approaches them from the standpoint of existence, then existence constitutes their essence;
if one approaches them from the standpoint of non-existence, then non-existence constitutes their essence. Now, I say they are not identical.
If you claim that a single principle follows two perspectives, is it one principle followed by two perspectives, or are there two principles followed by two perspectives? If it is...
If there were one principle, it would constitute a single truth; if there were two principles, they ought to have two distinct essences.

[The opponent claims] that the Middle Way within the two truths constitutes the essence, with existence and non-existence as its meanings. Now, I say this is not so; for how could these two exist while being combined into the essence of this Middle Way?
The dual functions of existence and non-existence must either exist apart from this Middle Way, or they must be conjoined with it.

If they were conjoined with this Middle Way, there should be only a single function, not two. If these two functions existed apart from this Middle Way, then once the Middle Way has been separated from them, it would no longer be the Middle Way;
consequently, the Two Truths would each possess their own distinct substance. How could they then be said to share the same [basis]?

The essence [of this teaching] is the One Middle Way. Although there are five interpretations, they ultimately reside within four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The first interpretation takes the proposition of existence as its essence.

The second interpretation takes the proposition of non-existence as its essence. The third and fourth interpretations represent the "half-existence, half-non-existence"; thus, the third proposition takes non-existence as its essence.
The fifth interpretation takes that which is neither existent nor non-existent as the [fourth proposition].
The four propositions constitute its essence. Now, in clarifying the essence of the two truths, how could one seek it by means of the four propositions?

In the teachings clarified here in the Mahāyāna, the essence of the two truths is merely a provisional designation. It is like the case of Tilapāyi, who in reality did not eat oil, yet was forcibly named "Oil-Eater.
The clarification that the essence of the two truths as a provisional name is likewise so is what has been transmitted from Guanzhong and Hexi.
Regarding the skillful means of the two truths: they are fundamentally intended to manifest the One Way;
if they were not for the purpose of manifesting the One Way, there would be nothing to discuss. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"Just as the Nanda Dragon King, out of compassion for sentient beings, emerges from the great ocean and rains down a great rain, so too does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, emerge from the great ocean of compassion and rain down [the Dharma]."
Regarding "Dharma": the rain of Dharma refers to the teaching-gates of the two truths (*satya*), wherein that which is capable of being realized constitutes truth.

According to the explanations of conventional teachers and the like: because existence exists, it exists; existence further manifests existence. Because non-existence is non-existent, it is non-existent; non-existence further manifests non-existence.

Since non-existence further manifests non-existence, the name "non-existence" resides only in non-existence. Since existence further manifests existence, the name "existence" resides only in existence.
Since existence and non-existence here merely indicate existence and non-existence themselves, existence and non-existence cannot indicate the Path.

Because they cannot indicate the Path, they are not termed "teachings on principle" (*li-jiao*). Now, it is clarified that there is no separate essence for the two truths; the sūtras do not speak of a distinct essence for the two truths.
Yet, what is being distinguished now is for the sake of clarifying the essence of the two truths for others; this is addressed in response to that treatise.
Now, it is said that the names of the two truths are provisional designations (*prajñapti*). A name lacks the power to apprehend a thing; yet it is also the provisional designation of a substance.

Since the substance has no correspondence to the name, it is not the name, nor is it the substance. It is merely because of its function that the substance is revealed as provisional, and because of the substance that its function is distinguished.

Provisional designations are called "existence"; provisional designations are called "non-existence. Provisional designations are called non-existence, which is termed "existence-and-non-existence. Provisional designations are called...

Because there is existence, one speaks of non-existence; non-existence is not existence, and existence is not non-existence. That which is neither existence nor non-existence is provisionally named "substance" (tattva).
This clarifies that existence and non-existence are provisionally named as "function. This is intended to indicate that which is neither true nor conventional.

Since that which is neither true nor conventional is forcibly and provisionally named "substance," how could it be said to exist? Therefore, the teaching on the existence and non-existence of causes and conditions serves to indicate that which is neither existent nor non-existent.
The Way is beyond existence. Thus, "existence" is taught to signify that it is not existent, and "non-existence" is taught to signify that it is not non-existent.
Therefore, these two teaching gates of existence and non-existence indicate the Way that is neither existent nor non-existent.

If one attains awakening to the Way that is neither existent nor non-existent by means of existence and non-existence, then the two teachings of existence and non-existence will vanish without a trace; they are merely provisional names for the Principle, or what is called the "Middle."

The Path, and so forth, including various names such as "correct contemplation" (samyak-darśana)—how could these not further constitute the essence of the Two Truths through the principle of neither existence nor non-existence?
By taking existence and non-existence as causes, one awakens to that which is neither existent nor non-existent; this is therefore called the Middle Way and correct contemplation.

When the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* elucidates the Middle Contemplation (*madhyama-vīpaśyanā*), it is precisely to clarify existence and non-existence and to manifest the correct contemplation of neither existence nor non-existence; for this reason, it is called "correct."

Because it is contemplation, it is called "right contemplation" (samyag-darśana). Based on this right contemplation, the three modes of intensity—clear, dim, and so forth—are metaphorically designated as the superior and inferior qualities of the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
If one first breaks through the views of eternalism and nihilism, that is called the first stage.

If eternalism and nihilism never arise again, it is called the contemplation of right contemplation; if it is purified, it is called the tenth stage. Now, I shall clarify the two teachings of existence and non-existence.
This expresses the principle that [the ultimate] is neither existent nor non-existent; therefore, it can be said that the two truths are of one essence (*eka-tattva*).
Because the former masters held that existence and non-existence are dual, they could not discern their single essence. Thus, we now clarify that the two truths take non-duality as their essence.
The two truths are existence and non-existence; non-duality is neither existence nor non-existence. It is precisely because duality is non-dual that there is duality; this duality is...
Because non-duality is duality, this is the function of the non-duality of the two truths. Because non-duality is not non-duality, it is non-duality because of duality.
This non-duality is duality because it is the non-duality of duality; this non-duality is the essence of the two truths. This is precisely the essence.

It is also called "principle" (li), it is also called "the middle" (zhong), and it is also called "the source" (ben). Its function is also called "teaching" (jiao), it is also called "provisional" (jia), and it is also called "not yet" (wei);

each has its respective counterpart, and for this reason these names are established. As for the name, the essence is not existent, yet there is an essence; the essence is not non-existent, yet there is no essence.
Bringing these two together to examine the essence, one also speaks of "two essences": taking that which is not existent as one essence, and that which is not non-existent [as the other].
They constitute a single essence. If one considers them from the perspective of this single essence, even what is called "one function" is likewise a conventional designation of function.
Question: What textual evidence proves that the two truths are merely teachings? Answer: The *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, in the chapter on "Contemplating Nature," states:
"By means of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one can speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). If one does not rely upon conventional truth, one cannot speak of the ultimate truth."
If one cannot speak of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), then one cannot attain nirvāṇa. Furthermore, it is said:
"If one wishes to know the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), one knows the ultimate truth; if one knows the ultimate truth, one knows the conventional truth. It is also said:
"The dependent origination of all Buddhas is called the profound ultimate truth. Because this is dependent origination, we know that the two truths are the teaching.

Furthermore, the *Catuhsatyaparivarta* states: "Although all phenomena are without arising, there are two truths. Another sutra says: "The Tathāgata constantly practices the Middle Way and teaches 'existence' for the sake of sentient beings.
Question: Is it stated in the sutras and śāstras that the two truths and the Middle Way constitute the essence [of reality]?
The *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-mūla-karma-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states: "As for the meaning of the two truths, they are neither one nor two;
neither eternal nor annihilated; neither coming nor going; neither arising nor ceasing. Yet these two aspects are identical, because the sages know them to be non-dual.
This is why all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know [the Dharma] as their mother. Furthermore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The essence of Nirvāṇa..."

It is neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is both existent and non-existent. Therefore, it is now clarified that not only the two truths, but also *nirvāṇa* and the Buddha-nature (*buddhatā*), all have the Middle Way as their essence.
As the preface to the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā-vṛtti* by Qingmu states:

"Sentient beings of the末法 (final dharma) age, upon hearing of non-arising, non-ceasing, and ultimate emptiness, immediately lose [the understanding of] the two truths. Thus, we know that the Master of the Treatise’s realization and understanding were...
Arising is non-extinction; thus, it possesses the two truths (*satyadvaya*). Furthermore, the *Catuhsatyaparivarta* states:
"Although all phenomena are without arising, there are still the two truths. Master Sengzhao’s treatise says: "When things have not yet come into being, they are neither existent nor non-existent.

Being neither existent nor non-existent, they constitute the substance of existence and non-existence, establishing all dharmas. Thus, the two truths receive their names through mutual dependence; they do not exist as distinct entities."

Because it is only when an entity (*tattva*) is designated as being either existent or non-existent that one can discuss mutual dependence (*apekṣā*). Since the entity itself is neither existent nor non-existent, it is not discussed in terms of mutual dependence.
Now, I shall provide three scriptural passages as evidence. First, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Dharmas have no comparison, for they lack mutual dependence;
dharmas have no causal attribution, for they do not abide in conditions. This clarifies the dharma of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Second, the *Mahā-...* [text continues].
The Sūtra says: "For example, great space is not called 'great space' because of small space; Nirvāṇa is likewise not called 'the Great Mark' because of small marks.
This refers to the name and essence as the Great Nirvāṇa. In the third [chapter] of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the "Examination of Fire and Fuel," it says:
"If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent. This was based on functional utility; now, however, there is none.
Regarding dependence: there is likewise no dharma that is established. This refers to their essential nature (*tattva*).

Although a general classification may be made in this manner, if one further discusses its meaning, there are four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). First, regarding the use of dependence and non-dependence, there are again four propositions.
The first is that duality involves dependence, while non-duality is non-dependent. For example, form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) constitute a duality; when discussing them...
Regarding "dependence": form and emptiness are non-dual. One does not discuss their dependence; one discusses their mutual identity (*samasatya*).

The meaning of dependence is subsumed. Within these two, there is again the sense of dependence and non-dependence. If one employs the two names "existence" and "non-existence," they are mutually dependent.

If one employs the two names "form" and "emptiness," they are not mutually dependent. Why? It is precisely because existence must depend on non-existence, and non-existence must depend on [existence].
There is. If one applies the name "form" (*rūpa*), it does not necessarily depend on "space" (*ākāśa*); it may also depend on dharmas such as mind (*citta*).

If one applies the name "space," it does not necessarily depend on form; it may also depend on mind and so forth. Thirdly, if one says that space depends on non-space, this is precisely a case of dependence (*apekṣā*).

If one says that emptiness depends upon existence, it conversely becomes non-dependent. The reason for this is that it is precisely by means of mutual dependence that all phenomena are conventionally designated;
thus, all phenomena obtain their status through dependence. If emptiness must necessarily depend on existence, then existence would not necessarily be present upon all phenomena.
This is like names that are established in relation to specific counterparts—such as "permanent," "self," "vase," or "garment"—whereas for others, there is no distinct counterpart. If...
To posit emptiness as depending on non-emptiness is to have dependence while lacking existence; this is to lack a dharma and thus fail to attain it.

Thus, the permanent depends upon the impermanent, and so on, even down to clothing and the absence of clothing. Fourth, if one says that emptiness depends on [non-emptiness] to constitute the non-emptiness of emptiness, this is indeed dependence.
If one simply says that emptiness depends on non-emptiness, this is not dependence. Therefore, there is no necessity for mutual correspondence.
Regarding "waiting": it is like saying that a garment waits for what is not a garment. Why must this necessarily refer to a finished garment as opposed to a non-garment?

Now, regarding the mutual completion of the [two] aspects of the Path (*mārga-lakṣaṇa*), it is only through their mutual dependence that they are established; therefore, the character "completed" (*cheng*) is added, for only then does the expression become complete.
These four types all clarify that within function there is both waiting and non-waiting. If the essence of the Middle Way is neither dual nor non-dual, it is emptiness.

It is not empty; therefore, it is neither dependent nor non-dependent. The second stage states that within function there is both dependence and non-dependence, and these two together are within the state of dependence.
Within essence there is neither dependence nor non-dependence, and these two together are non-dependent.
The reason for this is as follows: when one employs the "middle" (the Middle Way), there is both dependence and non-dependence.

Non-dependence is itself a form of dependence; thus, dependence and non-dependence together constitute a "great dependence. Since the essence (the Middle) is neither dependent nor non-dependent, it is the non-dependence of non-dependence and the dependence of non-dependence;
thus, essence and appearance together constitute a "great non-dependence. The third stage says: "To employ the function without yet looking toward the essence."
Both essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*) are dependent. If one takes essence as the standard to look toward function, then both function and essence are non-dependent.
The reason for this is that, since we are discussing dependence, that which is dependent cannot depend upon itself; it must depend upon essence.

Since both essence and function are dependent, and since essence is said to be non-dependent, it does not depend upon function. Although function is said to be dependent, upon whom does this dependence ultimately rely? Therefore...
In terms of their essence, both are non-contingent. The fourth stage states: "Although both essence and function are indeed contingent, the designation 'contingent' ultimately resides in function.

Although both essence and function are indeed non-contingent, the designation 'non-contingent' ultimately resides in essence. The reason for this is that one constantly brings the meaning of function to apply it to essence;
thus, one says "essence is contingent. But when has essence ever been contingent? Therefore, the designation "contingent" ultimately resides [in function].
Regarding function: since one always takes the meaning of the essence as the basis for function, it is said that [function] does not depend [on anything else].

Yet, when has function ever not depended [on the essence]? Thus, its independence ultimately resides within the essence. Question: If the ultimate and the conventional have no two distinct essences, how can one speak of "entering" or "emerging" from contemplation?

Answer: When one’s right contemplation realizes that the Way is neither existent nor non-existent, this is called "entering contemplation. If one remains in a mind of annihilationism or eternalism, one is not performing contemplation.
This is called "emerging from contemplation. The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "One who loves the merit of the Buddha is not called one free from afflictions," up until the seventh stage (*bhūmi*).

If one were to establish distinctions where there are none, and define "entering" and "emerging" from contemplation based on speech and silence or movement and stillness, then from the first generation of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), the Buddha has already distinguished between entering and emerging from contemplation.
Regarding the question of those who maintain two truths: it is possible for them to contemplate both simultaneously.

"You lack the principle of the two truths; how then can you observe them simultaneously? Answer: "I speak of 'simultaneous observation' because I rely on two conditions to observe both the teachings of existence and non-existence together;

thus, it is called 'simultaneous. Furthermore, regarding the meaning clarified in the Mahāyāna: it is not through the ultimate (paramārtha) that the conventional (saṃvṛti) is clarified, nor is it through the conventional that the ultimate is clarified.

Therefore, it is said that once the conventional is explained, the ultimate is established; once the ultimate is explained, the conventional is made clear. Thus, by understanding the conventional, one realizes the ultimate."

True. To realize the ultimate (paramārtha-satya) is itself to clarify the conventional (saṃvṛti-satya); therefore, it may be called "contemplating both together. In the conventional, there is the ultimate; in the ultimate, there is the conventional.

Thus, according to schools such as the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, since the ultimate and the conventional are distinct, one who realizes the ultimate will ultimately not understand the conventional, and one who awakens to the conventional will ultimately not understand the ultimate.
Since the ultimate and the conventional are not mutually related in this way, how could there be the meaning of "contemplating both together"? This awakening is neither existent... [text fragment]

For one who has no [fixed] path, what further "conformity" or "non-conformity" could there be? The question is asked so that by speaking of existence one may awaken to non-existence, and by speaking of non-existence one may awaken to non-non-existence.

As for the Path that is neither existent nor non-existent, wherein even existence and non-existence do not exist—how does this differ from the meaning of Emperor Liang Wu’s dream of flowers in the void, where upon awakening there were no flowers? Why is this so? Because he [the Emperor] clarified that birth and death are...

It is merely a great dream; therefore, one perceives the myriad phenomena of the universe. If one attains Buddhahood, it is like a Great Awakening, wherein one no longer perceives the existence of any dharmas whatsoever.
You now speak of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which exists for ordinary beings;

yet when one attains the state of a Sage, one realizes that this "existence" ultimately does not exist at all—this is precisely what is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). How is this different from that [which you previously asserted]?

[Question: Is there a difference? Furthermore, the doctrine of the Mountain Gate (Shanmen) generally holds that ordinary beings take existence as fundamental, while the Sages take non-existence as fundamental.

Now, if it is said that the ordinary person’s realization of existence indicates that it is not [ultimately] existent, and the Sage’s realization of non-existence indicates that it is not [ultimately] non-existent—this being called the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—then how does this differ from the realization of the Ultimate Truth where there is no longer any conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)? [Answer: ... (The answer follows).
The ancient interpretations differ. Some say that although one attains the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one does not lose the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

however, the conventional truth is merely provisional and possesses no further reality, like the *śaluka* (lotus root) of a mouse. Others say there are two truths, existence and non-existence, which are discussed in terms of their total substance (*sarva-ātmaka*), similar to how a melon is entirely submerged and entirely emerged [in water].
Below, the explanations of various masters will be explained in detail. Now, regarding the Mahāyāna doctrine:
Regarding the Two Truths: while the words appear similar, their meanings differ, transcending and standing far apart from the other. Why is this? Emperor Wu of Liang said:
"Because there is the affliction of delusion below the adamantine mind, there are the various phenomena of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);

when Buddhahood is attained, there is only the real and no mundane. Now, I say this is not so. If, upon attaining the fruit of Buddhahood, there were only the real and no mundane, then as for the [phenomena] that flow forth...

First: Is it that the mundane lacks the real? If one reaches Buddhahood, there is only the real. If the Truth of Reality (*tattva-satya*) were not a fruit, how could the myriad practices (*sādhana*) induce it?
If the fruit of Buddhahood were merely emptiness (*śūnyatā*), then emptiness would lack the capacity for illumination, and thus it would not be the locus of the transformative path.

Now, it is clarified that ordinary beings claim things exist substantially; once they have attained sainthood, they realize that what exists is ultimately non-existent. This state is identical [to the previous], yet it is also...
It does not lose its status as a provisional existence; therefore, it differs from that [other view]. Question: If that is so, what is the difference between this and what they also say?

Answer: They clarify that what exists as a provisional name truly exists. Now, I maintain that what is provisionally existent is not [ultimately] existent. How can these two be compared? It is precisely because of these various statements [that they differ].

This distinguishes [this teaching] from other schools. Now, it is clarified that for ordinary people who perceive existence, one speaks of "non-existence"; for sages who perceive non-existence, one speaks of "non-non-existence.

Just as an ordinary person does not realize they are dreaming until they attain the state of a sage and awaken, so too, upon awakening, one realizes that what was perceived as existing is no longer existent, and one realizes that what was perceived as non-existent is not truly non-existent.
Thus, by means of existence and non-existence, one attains that which is neither existent nor non-existent—neither ordinary nor sage.
This is the path that is neither dream nor waking; it is the skillful teaching regarding the existence and non-existence of consciousness. Therefore, it differs from other interpretations. Question:

If one wishes to lead sentient beings to realize the path that is neither existent nor non-existent, and thus speaks of existence and non-existence, why not speak directly of the path that is neither existent nor non-existent, rather than speaking of existence and non-existence as a skillful means? Answer: This was explained previously under the section on "Defining the Names."

This question has already been raised previously; it is now being addressed once more. The previous explanation concerned the indeterminacy of names, whereas the present one clarifies the indeterminacy of the essence (tattva);
thus, the intent behind each is distinct. Why is this? [The former] clarifies the causes and conditions for the Sage’s teaching, as well as whether those conditions are complete or incomplete.

[The latter] clarifies that while ordinary beings fundamentally believe "this exists" and "that exists," the Sage maintains that all phenomena (dharmas) are non-existent. For now, we shall provisionally accord with their [the ordinary beings'] discourse.

Regarding existence and non-existence: next, one must cause them to realize that existence is not existence—that which exists is non-existent—and that non-existence is not non-existence—that which is non-existent is existent.
Because non-existence is existent, it is not existence; because existence is non-existent, it is not non-existence.
Only then can one realize the Way that is neither existence nor non-existence. Question: Among the three types of Middle Way, there should be three Truths. Now, as for the True [Truth]...

Regarding the statement that "the Way which is neither mundane nor real transcends the mundane," should it also consist of the three truths? Answer: The three kinds of middle way are as explained in the section on the "Eight Negations.
However, while those [teachings] contain the principles of the two truths—the real and the mundane—they also contain the principle of the middle way that is neither real nor mundane.
Thus, in terms of doctrinal exposition, there are three truths. Here, we clarify that the real and the mundane are the teachings used to manifest the Way that is neither real nor mundane.

There is no separate principle for the two truths; how could there be three principles? Furthermore, when the two teachings designate [phenomena] as "truths," the underlying principle is not yet itself a truth.
When this expressed principle receives the name "truth," the names "truth" applied by the two teachings are set aside. What need is there for three truths?
Nevertheless, in accordance with conditions, one may also speak of three truths. Thus, the *Bodhisattva-ābharaṇa-mūla-karma-sūtra*, lower fascicle, states: "Wisdom has three objects."
First, illumination of the truth of existence; second, illumination of the truth of non-existence; third, illumination of the Middle Way, the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). Question:

Regarding those in the world who delight in inferior teachings—those of dull faculties who take pleasure in inquiring about the Two Truths of the Mahāyāna—how does this differ from the Kai-shan school?
Answer: These are ignorant people. They have not yet entered the nectar-like Dharma-gate of the Mahāyāna; they merely cling to their own views and say [it is otherwise].
It is so. It is like the case of a private person who was imprisoned by the authorities; if he were to realize the flavor of the Mahāyāna, he would surely mock his former stupidity.
The principle of the two truths according to the Kaishan school is a natural realm (*dharmatā*). Now, I clarify that the two truths are a teaching (*deśanā*).
In their school, the two truths are the aspect of the oneness of principle: one is formless, one is arising, and one is non-arising. Now I say that both are arising, and both are non-arising.
Arising. One arising and one non-arising; one non-arising and one arising. These four propositions. Regarding that meaning, the two truths are explained in one way and not explained in another.
Now, according to our intention, the two truths may also be explained through these four propositions or not explained. In that meaning, the ultimate truth is nameless.
There is a conventional name for this; it refers to the four propositions concerning "both being named" and so forth. In that school, of the two truths, one is provisional and one is non-provisional;
here, it is clarified that both are provisional. In that school, the two truths are principles (*li*); here, it is maintained that one truth is a phenomenon (*shi*).

Regarding their doctrine of the two truths, one is a borrowed name and one is not a borrowed name; regarding the two truths, one is a name applied by way of metaphor and one is not a name applied by way of metaphor. Now...

"Clarifying" (ming) refers to the essence of the name. When the holy wisdom (*āryajñāna*) of that school accords with the true realm (*bhūtārtha*), it reaches a state of ultimate forgetting yet remains ever-present.

Therefore, one can only speak of the mind giving rise to suffering; one cannot say that the True Principle gives rise to the function of affliction. This is because the capacity to oppress and the object oppressed are known to be distinct from non-wisdom (*ajñāna*).
Therefore, that treatise states: "The Sage enters the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) to temporarily suspend his labors.

Now, I say that both subject and object are simultaneously stilled; it is neither subject nor object. Thus, a sutra says: "To know that suffering is not suffering is called the Noble Truth of Suffering," and so forth. Where, then, could two natures possibly exist?

In that school, the principle of reality (tattva) is the ultimate (paramārtha), and the principle of empty penetration is the conventional (saṃvṛti). These two principles are fixed in their respective positions, remaining as dead ends.

Therefore, it is now said that the ultimate is spoken of as the conventional, and the conventional is spoken of as the ultimate; that the object is spoken of as wisdom, and wisdom is spoken of as the object.
That school possesses this principle of being nameless and signless (*animitta*). If this principle did not exist, it would constitute the nihilistic view of denial;
one could certainly not weigh it as a principle of non-existent reality. It is like saying there is a deity upon a tree, yet one cannot determine its trunk, branches, or leaves.
Regarding the existence [of things]: we now maintain that principles are elucidated through phenomena. Where, then, does such a principle exist?

If you say this is identical to the Two Truths theory of the Kaishan school, are you not indeed a person lacking in discernment? Furthermore, various masters such as those of the Kaishan school have unanimously declared with one voice that the ultimate principle is neither existent nor non-existent.
Now, the doctrine clarified by the Mahāyāna is that the principle is neither existence nor non-existence. If it were a principle...

This is neither existence nor non-existence; it is the principle that can be applied to what is to be applied. Now, to clarify that neither existence nor non-existence is itself the principle means there is no principle that can be applied.

If there were a principle that could be applied, then because that principle is a principle, it would be a principle [of principles]. Therefore, it is said that there is no principle that can be applied;

this is the principle of the principle that is not a principle. If a principle were a principle by virtue of being a principle, then the principle would possess a distinct principle that differentiates it from what is not a principle.

There is that which is irrational and distinct from the rational. Now it is clarified that the rational is the rationality of the irrational; there is no irrationality distinct from the rational, nor is there a rationality distinct from the irrational.

If there were a rationality distinct from the irrational and an irrationality distinct from the rational, then non-existence would not relate to existence, and non-non-existence would not relate to non-existence.
Now it is said that there is no rationality distinct from the irrational, nor irrationality distinct from the rational. That which is non-existent is precisely...
There is. That which is not non-existent is itself non-existence.
Section Eight: Discerning the Severance of Names.
*Wuyi wude dacheng sishu xuanyi ji*, Fascicle Five.
On the sixth day of the twelfth month of the third year of Xianqing, in the year of Wushu (59th year of the sexagenary cycle),
the monk Fa’an of Xinglun Monastery respectfully presented this "Chapter on Meaning" for the sake of the Great Emperor and those deceased within the inner palace.
Record of the Profound Meaning of the Four Mahāyāna Treatises: No-Reliance and No-Attainment, Scroll Six.

Regarding the meaning of "responsive resonance" (*ganying*), there are four sections: first, the general purport; second, the explanation of the names; third, the clarification of the essence and characteristics;
and fourth, the extensive analysis.

The first general meaning: Now, as for the principle of resonance (*ganying*), it refers precisely to the sense of mutual meeting, penetration, and interrelation between sentient beings and the Buddha;

its primary tenet is the flourishing and manifestation of the Buddha-dharma. Therefore, although the Perfected One has transcended names and marks (*nāman* and *lakṣaṇa*), [the principle of resonance remains].
Yet, when conditions arise, it must respond accordingly; according to what is appropriate, it manifests forms both coarse and subtle, and infinite shapes.
It does not fail to manifest through transformation because of its quiescent transcendence, nor does it diminish the Dharmakāya because of the cessation of its traces.
Thus, the "Chapter on the Four Marks" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "I have long dwelt in this Great Nirvāṇa, manifesting various supernatural powers and transformations."
This is explained in detail in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. Thus, it is only after long attaining nirvāṇa that one manifests inexhaustible transformation.

Therefore, both the true and the responsive must be clarified together to reveal the Middle Way of the True Dharma. As Master Zhaolun said: "Without the fundamental, there would be no way to manifest the traces;

without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental. Although the fundamental and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability. Furthermore, the Sūtra says: "In response to..."
The names used for these [terms] differ. In the first fascicle of the *A-vyavartaniya-sūtra*, Śāriputra and Ānanda ask the Buddha about the light he has seen and so forth.
What kind of resonance and response (*ganying*) is this? In other sūtras, some speak only of "resonance" (*gan*), while others speak only of "response" (*ying*).
The fiftieth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "To have no mind toward either self or other, yet to respond to all"—this is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

The *Ming jing* (Sutra on Illumination) states: "The Buddha’s true body is like empty space; it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water. The *Ruixing jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) says:

"Auspiciousness evokes a sign (*zheng*)," yet it does not explicitly mention "response" (*ying*). However, the meaning of "sign" (*zheng*) is precisely that of "response. A "sign" (*zheng*) refers to a portent.
If one explains the fundamental principle of resonance and response (*ganying*), then the worthy sages of the Two Vehicles serve as excellent fields for sentient beings; yet, in the Lesser Vehicle...
All seek their own expansion, not for the sake of sentient beings. Sentient beings who seek the Way must rely upon a vessel;

the greatness of such a vessel lies solely in the Bodhisattva. Because Bodhisattvas possess manifold skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and deliver others according to their capacities, they manifest various responsive transformations (*nirmāṇa*) within the realm of supreme goodness.
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, these manifested traces are particularly sublime; thus, they can manifest forms such as the sixteen-foot body. Therefore, it is great...
The *Sūtra on the Four Marks* states: "Hanging the ship of Nirvāṇa to enter into birth-and-death, he took Yaśodharā as his wife and begot Rāhula, thereby being able to accomplish the Great Task.
This refers to entering into birth-and-death; even though he relinquished his transformative influence at the Twin Trees, there is no loss in taking refuge [in him].

To clarify this meaning, the principle of response and resonance (*ganying*) is established. It differs from the conventional path, which, while dispelling the hundred negations, still maintains [existence].
Regarding the two bodies—the True Body and the Responsive Body—this treatise now clarifies that these two bodies are neither negated by the "not-hundred" nor affirmed by the "is-hundred";

they are two bodies established as provisional names through causes and conditions. Furthermore, there are three pairs of responses and inducements (*ganying*): first, universal and particular responses and inducements; second, corresponding and non-corresponding responses and inducements;
third, response and inducement regarding principle and phenomena. Within the category of universal and particular responses and inducements, [the universal]...
As for "resonance" (ganying): it is not that there are no sentient beings; where there are sentient beings, there must be a Buddha.

It is not that there is no Buddha; where there is a Buddha, there must be sentient beings. It is because of the Buddha that there are sentient beings; it is because of sentient beings that there is a Buddha.

If there is no Buddha, then there are no sentient beings; if there are no sentient beings, then there is no Buddha. Why is this? Where there is illness, there is medicine; where there are sentient beings, there must be a Buddha.
If there were no sentient beings, there would be no Buddha. For what purpose does a Buddha appear in the world? It is for the sake of sentient beings that he appears in the world.
Therefore, if there is no response, there can be no resonance. Furthermore, one would not know who these sentient beings are.
While one may feel a resonance with the Buddha before one’s death, it is still unknown which Buddha among all those who respond to sentient beings will appear before one.

For this reason, it is said that the principle of resonance and response is universal, without a specific point of affiliation. Furthermore, there is a sense in which resonance and response are universal. Why is this?

Since it was previously stated that sentient beings exist because of the Buddha, it can likewise be said that the Buddha exists because of sentient beings. If there were no sentient beings, the Buddha would not appear in the world.
Therefore, it is said that because of sentient beings there is a Buddha. Since these two "tusks" (causes) are mutually dependent, there is a mutual resonance between them.
While it was previously stated that the Buddha responds to sentient beings, now it is also seen that sentient beings who have attained the Way respond to the Buddha.

Furthermore, one does not know which particular sentient being first responds to the Buddha, nor how the Buddha first evokes the response of sentient beings; for this reason, it is universal and pervasive. Universal.

Regarding the meaning of "resonance" (*ganying*): what is taken as the basis for this resonance? We take the preceding sense of resonance as the basis. The Buddha is the "respondent" (*ying*) and sentient beings are the "stimulator" (*gan*). Question:

If it is said that sentient beings respond to the Buddha and the Buddha stimulates sentient beings—such that their mutual resonance is like the sprouting of a seed—then in that case, sentient beings would be the stimulators and the Buddha the respondent.
This principle is understandable; however, the Buddha is not a stimulator, while sentient beings are... [the text here is incomplete].
Regarding "responding" (*ying*): there should be three difficulties [to this]. First difficulty: Since sentient beings come to respond to the Buddha, the Buddha must have suffering and afflictions;
therefore, sentient beings must come to respond in order to rescue him. But since the Buddha has no sin or suffering, why would he need sentient beings to respond to him?
If one possesses the suffering of transgressions, one is bound by them oneself; how then could one untie the bonds of others? The answer has two meanings.
First, why must the Way necessarily involve responding to calamities? If the Buddha responds to sentient beings, that constitutes a response to calamity and a salvation from suffering.

If one says that sentient beings come to respond to the Buddha, this does not mean they go to meet him to rescue him from hardship or save him from suffering. As the first fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
when the Buddha was about to enter nirvana, he emitted light to summon those sentient beings with whom he had a karmic connection.

Thus, the Buddha is the one who evokes the response, and the sentient beings are those who come to respond to the Buddha. Such an interaction of resonance and response is not an instance of responding to or meeting someone in distress. Second, the answer following [the objection].

[Objection: It is difficult [to maintain this]. If the Buddha is bound, how could he untie the bonds of others? This is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the standpoint of therapeutic treatment) for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
The Buddha is neither bound nor unbound; yet, being neither bound nor unbound, he sometimes acts as if bound for the sake of delivering sentient beings.
As stated in the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: "I accept nine kinds of non-retribution. Furthermore, it is like when Jīvaka applied a needle to the Buddha’s head.
The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "I receive this body of the five aggregates; it is like receiving a red-hot iron ball, which cannot be endured for even a moment.

Such instances as these are all the suffering possessed by the Buddha. This serves as the condition (*pratyaya*). Therefore, it is said that there is bondage. In relation to the condition, this is bondage.

However, the Buddha has never been bound; he does not bind that which is unbound, just as one might apply names and marks to that which is nameless and markless so that sentient beings may recognize what is nameless and markless.
Furthermore, there are times when he is not bound by conditions or the path; yet the Buddha has never been "unbound. Why is this?
If the Buddha were subject to bondage, one could speak of him being "unbound"; since he has never been bound, how could he be [said to be] unbound?
This is a binding [objection]. Regarding the two difficulties: if sentient beings respond to the Buddha, then sentient beings become Buddhas;

if sentient beings do not become Buddhas, then sentient beings do not respond to the Buddha. The answer is that this meaning also exists. There is no fixed method for responding to objections with skillful means; thus, there is no obstruction.
If one speaks according to the conventional sense, saying that Prince Siddhārtha was born in the royal palace, this is precisely "sentient beings becoming Buddhas. Now, however, it is said:

This is because the Buddha creates sentient beings; therefore, he is born in a royal palace. If it is the Buddha who creates sentient beings and manifests himself as being identical to them, how could it be that sentient beings create Buddhas?

If sentient beings were to manifest themselves as being identical to the Buddha, then the Buddha would possess the eighty minor marks (*aśīty-anuvyañjana*), and sentient beings would likewise possess the eighty minor marks and the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*). If sentient beings were to become Buddhas, that would simply mean a Buddha has appeared.
Outside the four gates of the city, [the people] did not recognize those who were old, sick, and so forth. Chandaka pointed them out, saying, "These are śramaṇas;

these are sentient beings who have become Buddhas. Regarding the three difficulties: if a sentient being were to correspond to a Buddha, then although that sentient being would possess all-knowledge (sarvajñatā) and the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma), the Buddha would not correspondingly possess all-knowledge. Since he would not possess all-knowledge...

What is meant by "this Buddha"? Sentient beings should be eternally abiding and attain eternal nirvana; the Buddha, conversely, should be suffering, empty, impermanent, and subject to birth and death.
Answer: There are indeed precedents for this. However, according to the principles of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* and other such treatises, this is certainly not tenable.
Now, it is unimpeded. The Buddha is neither eternal nor impermanent; yet he is both eternal and impermanent. The Buddha is neither possessed of wisdom nor devoid of wisdom;
yet he is both possessed of wisdom and devoid of wisdom. Therefore, the *Śāstra* says: "When I sat at the site of enlightenment, wisdom was unattainable.
Like an empty fist deceiving a small child, I have already delivered all beings"—this is the Buddha’s lack of wisdom. [The character for "rice" (米) with "qi" (企) minus "zhi" (止) and "tu" (土)]
The *Śāstra* states: "The Bodhisattva causes [beings] to attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). The Buddha was born in a royal palace and passed away between the twin trees;

this demonstrates that the Buddha is subject to impermanence, birth-and-death, suffering, and emptiness. Furthermore, the Buddha enters the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*) and takes on bodies within birth-and-death.

Moreover, as the *Sūtra of Auspicious Responses* (*Sūryodgama-sūtra*) says: "[The Bodhisattva] did not recognize the old man and the sick person outside the city gate, remaining silent for three years while being nursed with milk. These instances are all...
This Buddha lacks wisdom; he is not equal to Chandaka in wisdom. This Buddha is impermanent and lacks wisdom.
Thus, one realizes that this very [Buddha] is both permanent and impermanent, wisdom and folly, and this is both nirvana and samsara. As for those who speak of sentient beings possessing wisdom:
As stated above: since Chandaka was the Buddha’s attendant, it is said that sentient beings possess wisdom. Because they possess wisdom, it can also be said that they are themselves *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the distinction between the wisdom of ignorance and so forth, up to the distinction between *saṃsāra* and *nirvāṇa*.
However, whether the Buddha is ignorant or wise, he is always wise; whereas whether sentient beings are ignorant or wise, they are all ignorant. Thus it should be understood.

Depending on whether one is foolish or wise, it is neither inherently foolish nor inherently wise. Regarding what is called "distinctive resonance and response" (*ganying*): sentient beings possess an innate nature that returns to the source;

therefore, they are able to cast out evil and cultivate wholesome karma. The cultivation of good and evil relies upon superior conditions (*pratyaya*) to reveal the Right Path, enabling beings to receive the teaching and surely attain the return to the source.
Among internal causes (*hetu*) and external conditions, none are greater than this; therefore, one should cultivate [it].
Goodness responds to the ultimate Sage, and the ultimate Sage bestows his response to bring about wondrous goodness. It is only because conditions differ that this occurs:

if a particular being is to be inspired toward goodness, the Buddha will respond specifically to them, while other sentient beings do not see him. For example, in the city of Rājagṛha there were one billion two hundred million households;
four hundred million households neither heard nor saw the Buddha, four hundred million heard of him but did not see him, and [the remaining] four...

A hundred million households have both heard and seen this; thus, it is a distinct response. If one performs wholesome deeds and possesses the necessary conditions (*pratyaya*), the Buddha will respond and deliver them.

If there are no such conditions, the Buddha will not respond and will not deliver them. Question: If those who possess the conditions and cultivate wholesome deeds naturally attain deliverance, what is the use of establishing conditions?
Furthermore, if sentient beings lack the conditions and the Buddha does not respond to them, what is meant by [the Buddha’s] "response"?

The Buddha’s great compassion is all-pervasive toward sentient beings who lack a karmic connection. Among those within the six realms, the four modes of birth, and the midst of the eight sufferings, there are none whom he does not teach to save.
Furthermore, he possesses the Four Great Vows. If this is so, what is meant by "Buddha"? Answer:
This meaning is explained extensively in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. It is like a wind shaking a fruit tree: those that are ripe fall first; those that are unripe do not.
It is a fallacy. It is also like the old woman to the east of the city who could not be transformed by those around her; it is not that the Buddha lacks compassion.
Regarding what is called "correspondence" (*xiangying*) and "non-correspondence," if there is a good cause, it corresponds to a good result;
if there is an evil cause, it corresponds to an evil result. This is not clarified here. Now, correspondence and resonance are clarified: the capacity to resonate and that which is resonated...

Sensation. That which is capable of responding and that which is to be responded to are both in accord with the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Why is this? Regarding what sentient beings ought to do, these sentient beings penetrate the characteristics of dharmas;
they realize and understand the profound meaning, becoming conjoined with omniscience (*sarvajñā*). Their conduct and their studies are all in accord with the characteristics of dharmas.

The Buddha, too, has thoroughly penetrated the characteristics of dharmas. This is the capacity to respond and that which is to be responded to, both of which are in accord with the characteristics of dharmas.
"Correspondence" means that there is a mutual resonance and response. As for what is called "non-correspondence," it refers to deluded sentient beings who are confused about the Right Path;

therefore, they do not correspond with the characteristics of the Dharma. Only the characteristics of the Buddha-Dharma correspond [to reality], yet because sentient beings are inverted, they remain stagnant within the twenty-five realms of existence. Thus, the Buddha, out of great compassion, considers that sentient beings do not know all dharmas.
Emptiness. Because they do not know that their own bodies are empty, they recklessly conceive the views of "self" and "mine," thereby giving rise to afflictions.

Out of compassionate concern for such sentient beings, the Buddha comes to manifest in response to them. Question: Since they already possess the same knowledge of all phenomena as the Buddha and correspond to *sarvajñā* (omniscience), they are already Buddhas.
